body.text:
mahāsvetā tu tacchrutvā suciraṃvicārya "gaccha, svayamevāhamāgatya yathārhamācariṣyāmi' ityuktvā keyūrakaṃ prāhiṇot /
gate ca keyūrake candrāpīḍamuvāca-"rājaputra! ramaṇīyo hemakūṭaḥ, citrā ca citraratharājadhānī, bahukutūhalaḥ kimpuruṣaviṣayaḥ, peśalo gaṃndharvalokaḥ, saralahṛdayā mahānubhāvā ca kādambarī, yadā nātikhedakaramiva gamanaṃ kalayasi, nāvasīdati vā guruprayojanam, adṛṣṭacaraviṣayakutūhalivā cetaḥ, madvacanamanurudhyate <3> <3.asmadvacanam> vā bhavān sukhadāyi <4> <4.bhavanmatiratisukhadāyi, bhavanmatiḥ sukhadāyi> vā āścaryadarśanam,<1> <1.asmacciradarśanam> arhāmi vā praṇayami2> <2.arhasi vā praṇayamimam...praṇayam> , mamapratyākhyānayogyaṃ vā<3> <3.yogyāṃ vā manyase mām> janaṃ manyase, samārūḍho vā paricayaleśaḥ, anugrāhyo vāyaṃ janaḥ, tato nārhasi niṣphalāṃ kartumabhyarthanābhimām /
mayaiva<4> <4.kvacit "ita' ityadhikaḥ pāṭhaḥ samupalabhyate> saha gatvā hemakūṭamatiramaṇīyatānidhānam, tatra dṛṣṭvā ca mannirviśeṣāṃ kādambarīm,apanīya tasyāḥ kumati <5> <5.kumatimimām> manomohavilasitam, ekamaho viśramya śvobhūte pratyāgamipyasi /
mama hi niṣkāraṇabāndhavaṃ bhavantamālokyaiva duḥkhāndhakārabhārākrāntena mahataḥ kālāducchvasitamiva cetasā, śrāvayitvā svavṛttāntamimaṃ sahyatāmiva gataḥ śokaḥ /
duḥkhitamapi janaṃ ramayanti sajjanasamāgamāḥ /
parasukhopapādanaparādhīnaśca bhavādṛśāṃ guṇodayaḥ' ityuktavatīñcaināṃ candrāpīḍo 'vravīt-"bhagavati! darśanātprabhṛti paravānayaṃ janaḥ karttavyeṣu yatheṣṭamaśaṅkitatayā niyujyatām' ityabhidhāya tayā sahaivodacalat /
body.translated_text:
But <s>Mahāśvetā</s>, having heard that and having deliberated for a long time, said 'Go; I myself will come and act as is fitting,' and sent <s>Keyūraka</s> away.
When <s>Keyūraka</s> had gone, she said to <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>: 'O prince! <s>Hemakūṭa</s> is delightful, and wonderful is the capital of King <s>Citraratha</s>; the realm of the <s>Kimpuruṣas</s> is full of wonder; the world of the <s>Gandharvas</s> is charming; and <s>Kādambarī</s> is sincere-hearted and of great dignity. If you consider the journey not too troublesome, and if the business of your elders is not suffering, or if your mind is curious about the realm of unseen wonders, or if you accede to my request, or if the sight of marvels would bring you pleasure, or if I deserve affection, or if you consider this person not worthy of refusal, or if even a small acquaintance has grown, or if this person deserves your favor—then you should not render this entreaty of mine fruitless.
Going together with me to <s>Hemakūṭa</s>, that treasury of supreme beauty, and having seen there <s>Kādambarī</s>, who is no different from me [in affection toward you], having dispelled the play of delusion in her misguided mind, you will rest for a single day and return the next day.
For upon merely seeing you, who are a kinsman without cause to be so, my heart, overwhelmed by the burden of the darkness of sorrow, has as it were breathed again after a long time. Having made you hear this tale of mine, my grief has become, as it were, bearable. The gatherings of good people delight even the sorrowful. And the rise of virtues in persons like you is entirely devoted to bringing about the happiness of others.'
And to her who had spoken thus, <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> said: 'Noble lady! From the moment of seeing you, this person is at your disposal; command me without hesitation as you wish in matters to be done.' Having said thus, he set forth together with her.

krameṇa ca gatvā hemakūṭamāsādya gandharvarājakulam, samatītya kāñcanatoraṇāni saptakakṣāntarāṇi kanyāntaḥpuradvāramavāpa /
mahāśvetādarśanapradhāvitena dūrādeva kṛtapraṇāmena kanakavetralatāhastena <1> <1.dvārapālapratīhārī> pratīhārajanenopadiśaayamānamārgaḥ praviśya asaṃkhyayanārīśatasahasrasambādham <2> <2....sambādhaḥ> , strīmayamaparamiva jīvalokam, iyattāṃ grahītumekatra trailokyastraiṇamiva saṃgṛhītam <3> <3.saṃhṛtam> , apuruṣamiva sargāntaram, aṅganādvīpamivāpūrvamutpannam, pañcamamiva nārīyugāvatāram, aparāmava puruṣadveṣiprajāpatinirmāṇam, aneka-kalapa-kalpanārthamutpādya sthāpitamivāṅganākoṣam <1> <1....kośam> , ativistāriṇā yuvatijanalāvaṇyaprabhāpūreṇa plāvitadigantareṇa siñcatevāmṛtarasavisareṇa divasamārdrīkurvateva bhuvanāntarālaṃ bahula <2> <2.bahala...> -prabhāvarṣiṇā marakatamaṇimayena <3> <3.kvacidiha "bhūṣaṇeneva' ityadhikaḥ pāṭhaḥ upalabhyate> sarvataḥ parigatatayā tejomayamiva, candramaṇḍalasahasrairiva nirmitasaṃsthānam, jyotsnayeva ghaṭitasanniveśam, ābharaṇaprabhābhirivaniṣpāditadigantaram, vibhramairiva kṛtasarvopakaraṇam, yauvanavilāsairivotpāditāvayavam, rativilasitairiva racita <4> <4.viracita...> -sañcayam, manmathācaritairiva kalpitāvakāśam, anurāgeṇevānuliptasakalapradeśam <1> <1....praveśam> śṛṅgāramayamiva, saundaryamayamiva, suratādhidaivatamayamiva, kusumaśaramayamiva, kutūhalamayamiva, āścaryamayamiva, saukumāryamayamiva <2> <2.premamayamiva> , kumāraḥ kumārīpurābhyantaraṃ dadarśa /
atibahalatayā ca tasya kanyakājanasya samantādānanadyatibhirindubimbavṛṣṭimiva patantīm, apāṅgavikṣepaiścalitakuvalayavanamayīmiva kriyamāṇāmavanīm, anibhṛta <3> <3.abhinibhṛta...> -bhrūlatāvibhramaiḥ kāma-kārmuka-vilāsa śatānīva <4> <4.kāmakārmukabalānīva, śatāni, vilāsatā> pracalitāni, śarasijakalāpāndhakārairbahulapakṣa <5> <5.keśani> -pradoṣa-sārthāniva sambadhnataḥ, smitaprabhābhirutphullakusumadhavalāniva vasantadivasān sañcarataḥ, śvasitānilaparimalairmalayamārutāniva paribhramataḥ, kapolamaṇḍalokairmāṇikyadarpaṇasahasrāṇīva sphuritāni karatalarāgeṇa raktakamalavanavarṣiṇamiva jīvalokam, kararuhakiraṇasphuraṇena <1> <1.kararuhasphuraṇena> kusumāyudhaśarasahasrairiva saṃcchāditāni digantarāṇi <2> <2.saṃcchāditadigantarāṇi, saṃcchāditamaṣṭadigantam> , <3> <3.kiraṇanikara> ābharaṇakiraṇendrāyudhajālakairuḍḍīyamānānīva <4> <4.bhuvana> bhavanamayūravṛndāni, yauvanavikārairupādyamānānīva manmathasahasrāṇyadrākṣīt /
ucitavyāpāravyapadeśena kumārikāṇāṃ sakhīhastāvalambeṣu pāṇigrahaṇāni, veṇuvādyeṣu cumbanavyatikarān, vīṇāsu kararuhavyāpārān, kandukakrīḍāsu karatalaprahārān bhavana- <5> <5.bhuvana-> latā-seka-kalasa-kaṇṭheṣu bhujalatāpariṣvaṅgān, līlādolāsu nitamba-stana <6> <6....sthala...> -preṅkhitāni, <7> <7.kvacit "tāmbūla'-padaṃ na dṛśyate> tāmbūlavīṭikāvakhaṇḍaneṣu daśanopacārān, bakulaviṭapeṣu madhugaṇḍūṣapracārān <8> <8.bakulakusumadohadeṣu sīdhugaṇḍūṣapradānāni> , aśokatarutāḍaneṣu caraṇābhighātān, upahārakusumaskhalaneṣu sītkārān <9> <9.śītkārān> atiriktaṃ suratamivābhyasyantīnāmapaśyat /
yatra ca <1> <1.yasya ca> kanyakājanasya kapolatalāloka eva mukhaprakṣālanam, locanānyeva karṇotpalāni, hasitacchavaya evāṅgarāgāḥ, niśvāsāḥ <2> <2.niḥśvāsāḥ> evādhivāsagandhaprayuktayaḥ, adharadyutireva kuṅkumānulopanam <3> <3.kuṅkumamukhānulepanam> ālāpā eva tantrīninādāḥ, bhujalatā eva campakamālāḥ <4> <4.camkaṣaikakṣyamālāḥ> , karatalānyeva līlākamalāni, stanā evaṃ darpaṇāḥ, nijadehaprabhaivāṃśukāṣaguṇṭhanam, jananasthalānyeva vilāsamaṇiśilātalāni komalāṅgulirāga eva caraṇālaktakarasaḥ, nakhamaṇimarīcaya eva kuṭṭimopahārakusumaprakarāḥ /
yatra cālaktakaraso 'pi <5> <5.yatra cālaktaraso 'pi> caraṇātibhāraḥ, bakulamālikāmekhalākalanamapi gamanavighnakaram, aṅgarāgagauravamapyadhikaśvāsanimittam, aṃśukabhāro 'pi glānikāraṇam, maṅgalapratisaravalayavidhṛtirapi karatalavidhutihetuḥ, avataṃsakusumadhāraṇamapi śramaḥ, karṇapūra-kamala-madhukarapakṣa-pavano 'pyāyāsakaraḥ <1> <1.vāto 'pi> /
tathā ca yatra sakhīdarśaneṣva <2> <2.darśane 'pi> kṛtahastāvalambanamutthānamatisāhasam <3> <3.abhyutthānam> , prasādhaneṣu hārabhārasahiṣṇutā stanakārkaśyaprabhāvaḥ, kusumāvacayeṣu dvitīyakusuma <4> <4....puṣpa...> -grahaṇamapyayuvatijanocitam, kanyakāvijñāneṣu mālyagrathanam <5> <5.mālyagranthanam> asukumārajanavyāpāraḥ, devatāpraṇāmeṣu madhyabhāgabhaṅgo nātivismayakaraḥ /
tasya caivaṃvidhasya <1> <1....antaramavakramya> kiñcidabhyantaramatikramya itaścetaśca paribhramataḥ kādambarīpratyāsanrasya parijanasya tāṃstānatimanoharānālāpān /
tathāhi-"lavalike! kalpaya ketakīdhūlibhirlavalīlatālavālamaṇḍalāni /
<2> <2.sārasike> sāgarike! gandhodaka-kanata-dīrghikāsu <3> <3.gandhodakadīrghikāsu, kanakanadikāsu> vikiraratnabālukām /
mṛṇālike! kṛtrimakamalinīṣu kuṅkumareṇumuṣṭibhiśchuraya <4> <4.kṣoda> <5> <5.kvacit "yantra'padaṃ nāsti> yantracakravākamithunāni <6> <6.yugalāni> nāni /
<7> <7.mandārike...> makarike! karpūrapallavarasenādhivāsaya gandhapātrāṇi /
rajanike! <8> <8.bhavanatamāla...bhavanadīrghikātamāla> tamāla-vīthikāndhakāreṣu nighehi <9> <9.maṇidīpān> maṇipradīpān /
kumudike! sthagaya <10> <10.rakṣaṇārtham> śakunikularakṣaṇāya muktājālairdāḍimīphalānānipuṇike! <11> <11.lekhaya> likha <12> <12.maṇistambhā...> maṇiśālabhañjikāstaneṣu kuṅkumarasapatrabhaṅgān /
utpalike! parāmṛśa kanakasammārjanībhiḥ <1> <1.kamalasammārjanībhiḥ, saṃmārjanībhiḥ> kadalīgṛhamarakatavedikām <2> <2.vedikāḥ> /
kesarike <3> <3.kusumike!> siñca madirārasena bakulakusumamālāgṛhāṇi /
mālatike! pāṭalaya sindūreṇunā kāmadevagṛhadantabalabhikām /
nalinike! pāyaya kamalamadhurasaṃ bhavanakalahaṃsān /
kadalike! naya dhārāgṛhaṃ gṛhamayūrān /
kamalinike! prayaccha cakravākaśāvakebhyo <4> <4.cakravākebhyaḥ> mṛṇālakṣīrarasam /
cūtalatike <5> <5.catūkalike!> dehi pañjarapuṃskokilebhyaścṛtakalikāṅkurāhāram /
pallavike! bhojaya maricāgrapallavadalāni bhavanahārītān /
lavaṅgike! vikṣipa <6> <6.nikṣipa> cakorapañjareṣu pippalītaṇḍula <7> <7.dala> -śakalāni /
madhukarike! viracayakusumābharaṇakāni /
mayūrike! saṅgītaśālāyāṃ visarjaya kinnaramithunāni /
kandalike! samārohaya krīḍāparvataśikharaṃ jīvañjīvamithunāni /
harimike! dehi pañjaraśukasārikāṇāmupadeśam' <8> <8....sārikopadeśam> ityetāni <9> <9.etāni> anyāni ca parihāsajalpitānyaśrauṣīt /
tathāhi-"cāmarike! mithyāmugdhatāṃ <1> <1.vṛthā> prakaṭayantī kamabhisandhātumicchami? ayi yauvanavilāsairumattīkṛte! <2> <2.jñātā> vijñātāsi, yā tvaṃ stana-kalasa-bhārāvanamyamānamūrttirmaṇistambhamayūrānālambase <3> <3....stambhamayūkhānavalambase> /
parihāsakāṅkṣiṇi! ratnabhittipatitamātmapratibimbamālapasi <4> <4....pratimāmālapayasi> /
pavanahṛtottarīyāṃśuke! hāraprabhāyāsitakaratalā saṅkalayasi <5> <5.ākalayasi> /
maṇikuṭṭimeṣūpahārakamalaskhalanabhīte! nijamukhapratibimbakāni pariharasi /
nijasaukumāryya-kharvita-bisaprasūna-saubhāgye! <6> <6.kvacit "nijasokumārya...ityārabhya "jāla' paryantaṃ na vidyate /
kvacicca sampūrṇasambodhanāntameva padaṃ na dṛśyate> jālavātāyanapatitapadmarāgālokaṃ <1> <1.avalokam> prati bālātapaśaṅkayā <2> <2.āśaṅkīnī> karatalamātapatrīkaroṣi /
kheda-srasta <4> <4.khedagrasta...> -hastagalita-cāmare <5> <5.kalitacāmarā, kalitacāmaraiḥ> ! <6> <6.kiraṇa...> nakhamuṇimayyūkhakalāpamādhunoṣi' ityetānyanyāni ca śṛṇlanneva kādambarībhavanasamopam upayayau <7> <7.bhavanamupasṛtya yayau, bhavanamupayayau> /
pulināyamānamupavanalatā-galita-kusuma-reṇu-paṭalaiḥ, durddināyamānanibhṛta-parabhṛta-nakhakṣatāṅga <8> <8...kṣatāṅgana...> -sahakāraphala-rasa-varṣaiḥ, nīhārāyamāṇamalina-viprakīrṇairvakula-seka-sīdhu-dhārā-dhūlibhiḥ, kāñcanadvīpāyamānaṃ campakadalopahāraiḥ <1> <1.campakopahāraiḥ> , nīlāśoka <2> <2.līlāśoka...> -vanāyamānaṃ kusuma-prakara-patita-madhukarabṛndāndhakāraiḥ, tathā ca sañjarataḥ <3> <3.sañcaran> strījanasya rāgasāgarāyamāṇaṃ caraṇālaktakarasavisaraiḥ, amṛtotpattidivasāyamānamaṅgarāgāmodaiḥ, candralokāyamānandantapatraprabhāmaṇḍalaiḥ, <4> <4.patramaṇḍalaiḥ> priyaṅguvanāya mānaṃ kṛṣṇāgurupatrabhaṅgaiḥ <5> <5.priyaṅguvanāyamānaṃ rocanātilakabhaktibhiḥ, nīlāyamānaṃ kṛṣṇāgurupatrabhaṅgaiḥ> , lohitāyamānaṃ karṇapūrāśokapallavaiḥ <6> <6.karṇāśokapallavaiḥ> , dhavalāyamānaṃ candanarasavilepanaiḥ, haritāyamānaṃ śirīṣakusumābharaṇaiḥ, atha sevārthamāgatenobhayata ūrdhvasthitena strījanena prākāreṇeva lāvaṇyamayena kṛtadīrgharathyāmukhākāraṃ mārgamadrākṣīt /
te cāntarnipatantam <7> <7.nipatitam> ābharaṇakiraṇālokaṃ sampiṇḍitaṃ nadīveṇikājalapravāhamiva vahantamapaśyat /
tanmadhye ca pratisrota iva gatvā pratīhārīmaṇḍalādhiṣṭhitapurobhāgaṃ śrīmaṇḍapaṃ dadarśa /
body.translated_text:
And proceeding gradually, having reached <s>Hemakūṭa</s> (the Golden Peak) and the royal household of the <s>Gandharva</s> king, passing through seven golden archways and enclosures, he arrived at the door of the maidens' inner quarters.
Shown the way by doorkeeper attendants who rushed forward at the sight of <s>Mahāśvetā</s>, making obeisance from afar, with golden cane-staffs in hand, he entered — and beheld the place thronged with countless hundreds of thousands of women, like another world made entirely of women, as though the femininity of the three worlds had been gathered together in one place to grasp its extent, like a creation-cycle without men, like an unprecedented continent of women that had newly arisen, like a fifth age consisting solely of women, like another creation by a <s>Prajāpati</s> who detested men, like a storehouse of womanhood produced and set aside for fashioning many garlands of creation — pervaded on all sides by a vast flood of the radiance of youthful beauty that inundated the quarters, as if sprinkling them with streams of nectar, as if moistening the space between the worlds by day with copious rays of splendor, appearing as if made of light due to being entirely surrounded by emerald gems, as though its structure were fashioned from thousands of moon-orbs, as though its arrangement were composed of moonlight, as though the horizons were produced by the radiance of ornaments, as though all its furnishings were made of coquetry, as though its parts were brought forth by the playfulness of youth, as though its contents were fashioned by the sports of love, as though its spaces were devised by the activities of <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love), as though its every surface were anointed with passion — seemingly made of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic sentiment), seemingly made of beauty, seemingly made of the presiding deity of love, seemingly made of the flower-arrowed one (<s>Kāmadeva</s>), seemingly made of curiosity, seemingly made of wonder, seemingly made of delicacy — the prince beheld the interior of the maidens' quarters.
And due to the great density of that host of maidens, he saw everywhere: a rain of moon-discs, as it were, falling from their joyful faces; the ground being made into a moving forest of blue lotuses, as it were, by the sidelong glances they cast; hundreds of <s>Kāma's</s> bow-sports, as it were, set in motion by the playful movements of their restless brow-creepers; the darkness of clusters of lotuses, as it were, binding together twilights of the dark fortnight from their tresses; days of spring made white with full-blown flowers, as it were, moving about from the radiance of their smiles; breezes from <s>Malaya</s> mountain, as it were, wandering about from the fragrance carried by the wind of their sighs; thousands of ruby mirrors, as it were, sparkling from the sight of the orbs of their cheeks; the world of the living raining red lotuses, as it were, from the redness of their palms; the horizons covered with thousands of the flower-weaponed one's arrows, as it were, from the flashing of the rays of their nails; flocks of the peacocks of existence, as it were, taking flight from the rainbow-nets of the rays of their ornaments; and thousands of <s>Manmathas</s> (Love-gods) being brought forth, as it were, by the transformations of youth.
Under the pretext of their proper occupations, among the maidens he observed: in the clasping of friends' hands, the taking of the hand (in marriage, as it were); in playing the flute, the intermingling of kisses (as it were); in playing the <s>vīṇā</s>, the employment of nails (as in love-scratching); in ball-games, the striking of palms (as in love-play); in embracing the necks of water-pitchers for watering the garden creepers, the embracing with vine-like arms (as in an embrace); on pleasure-swings, the swaying of hips and breasts; in the biting of betel-leaf preparations, the employment of teeth (as in love-bites); on <s>bakula</s> trees, the spraying of mouthfuls of liquor (as in the <s>bakula</s>-blooming rite); in striking <s>aśoka</s> trees, the kicking with feet (as in love-play); and in stumbling over offering-flowers, the hissing intakes of breath — as if they were practicing love-making to excess.
And there, among that host of maidens: the very sight of their cheek-surfaces served as face-washing; their eyes themselves were ear-lotuses; the luster of their smiles served as body-cosmetics; their sighs themselves served as perfume-fragrances; the glow of their lips served as saffron ointment; their speech itself was the sound of lute-strings; their vine-like arms were themselves <s>campaka</s>-garlands; their palms themselves were sport-lotuses; their breasts themselves were mirrors; the radiance of their own bodies served as silk garment-covering; their birthplaces themselves were pleasure-gem-slabs; the delicate redness of their fingers served as lac-dye for the feet; and the rays of their nail-gems served as offering-flower clusters on the floor.
And there, even lac-dye was too heavy a burden for their feet; even the fastening of a <s>bakula</s>-blossom girdle-chain was an impediment to walking; even the weight of body-cosmetics caused excessive breathing; even the burden of a garment was a cause of fatigue; even wearing auspicious thread-bracelets caused trembling of the palms; even wearing flowers as ear-ornaments was wearying; and even the breeze from the wings of bees on the lotuses worn as ear-ornaments was exhausting.
And furthermore, there: rising to greet friends with the support of a companion's hand was considered an extreme exertion; in adorning, the ability to bear the weight of necklaces was due to the hardness of the breasts; in flower-gathering, the picking of even a second flower was unbecoming to young maidens; in the accomplishments of maidens, garland-weaving was an activity unfit for those of such delicacy; and in bowing to deities, the bending of the waist was not overly surprising.
And having entered somewhat further into such a place as this, wandering here and there near <s>Kādambarī's</s> dwelling, he heard from the attendants various most enchanting utterances.
Namely: "<s>Lavalikā</s>! Arrange the circular basins of the <s>lavalī</s> creepers with <s>ketakī</s>-flower pollen!
<s>Sāgarikā</s>! Scatter gem-sand in the golden channels of perfumed water!
<s>Mṛṇālikā</s>! Sprinkle handfuls of saffron dust upon the mechanical <s>cakravāka</s> couples in the artificial lotus-ponds!
<s>Makarikā</s>! Perfume the incense-vessels with the juice of camphor leaves!
<s>Rajanikā</s>! Place gem-lamps in the darkness of the <s>tamāla</s> tree avenues!
<s>Kumudikā</s>! Cover the pomegranate fruits with pearl-nets to protect them from flocks of birds!
<s>Nipuṇikā</s>! Paint saffron leaf-patterns on the breasts of the gem-pillar statues!
<s>Utpalikā</s>! Sweep the emerald terrace of the plantain-house with golden brooms!
<s>Kesarikā</s>! Sprinkle the <s>bakula</s>-blossom garland-houses with wine!
<s>Mālatikā</s>! Redden the tooth-ledge of <s>Kāmadeva's</s> temple with vermilion!
<s>Nalinikā</s>! Give lotus-nectar to the palace swans!
<s>Kadalikā</s>! Take the palace peacocks to the fountain-house!
<s>Kamalinikā</s>! Give lotus-fiber milk to the <s>cakravāka</s> chicks!
<s>Cūtalatikā</s>! Give sprouting mango-bud food to the caged male cuckoos!
<s>Pallavikā</s>! Feed pepper-leaf tips to the palace <s>hārīta</s> birds!
<s>Lavaṅgikā</s>! Scatter pepper-and-rice fragments into the <s>cakora</s> bird cages!
<s>Madhukarikā</s>! Prepare flower-ornaments!
<s>Mayūrikā</s>! Release the <s>kinnara</s> couples into the music-hall!
<s>Kandalikā</s>! Set the <s>jīvañjīva</s> bird couples upon the peak of the pleasure-hill!
<s>Harimikā</s>! Give instruction to the caged parrots and <s>sārikā</s> birds!" — these and other such playful conversations he heard.
Namely: "<s>Cāmarikā</s>! Displaying false innocence, whom do you wish to deceive? O you who are intoxicated by the sports of youth — you are found out! You, whose figure bends under the weight of your pitcher-like breasts, are leaning against the pillar-peacocks!
O you who seek amusement! You are gazing at your own reflection fallen upon the gem wall!
O you whose upper garment has been carried off by the wind! With your palms darkened by the radiance of your necklace, you are adjusting (your garment)!
O you who fear stumbling over offering-lotuses on the gem floor! You are avoiding the reflections of your own face!
O you whose beauty humbles the loveliness of lotus-fiber blossoms by its own delicacy! Toward the ruby-light falling through the lattice window, you raise your palm as a parasol, suspecting it to be the heat of the young sun!
O you whose fan has slipped from your hand, loosened by fatigue! You are fanning yourself with the cluster of rays from your nail-gems!" — hearing these and other such remarks, he approached the vicinity of <s>Kādambarī's</s> dwelling.
And he saw a path made to look like the mouth of a long road, flanked on both sides by women who had come for attendance and stood above — like a rampart made of beauty — its ground made sandy, as it were, by the masses of pollen from flowers fallen from the garden creepers; made overcast, as it were, by showers of mango-fruit juice from the love-scratch marks on the hidden cuckoos' bodies; made misty, as it were, by the scattered droplets of wine sprinkled on <s>bakula</s> trees; made into a golden island, as it were, by offerings of <s>campaka</s> petals; made into a dark <s>aśoka</s> grove, as it were, by the darkness of swarms of bees fallen upon the heaps of flowers; and further, from the women passing through: made into an ocean of passion, as it were, by the streams of lac-dye from their feet; made into the day of the arising of nectar, as it were, by the fragrance of their body-cosmetics; made into the realm of the moon, as it were, by the circles of radiance from their teeth-decorations; made into a <s>priyaṅgu</s> forest, as it were, by black aloe leaf-patterns; reddened, as it were, by <s>aśoka</s> sprigs worn as ear-ornaments; whitened, as it were, by sandalwood paste ointments; made green, as it were, by <s>śirīṣa</s>-flower ornaments. Then he beheld, made in the form of a long street by the women standing on both sides above who had come for service — like a rampart made of beauty.
And he saw the light of ornament-rays falling within that path, flowing together like the water-current of a braided river.
And going, as it were, against that current, in the midst of it, he beheld the auspicious pavilion, its entrance attended by a circle of female doorkeepers.

āsīccāsya manasi-"śeṣendriyāṇyapi me vedhasā kimiti locanamayānyeva na kṛtāni /
kiṃ vānena kṛvamavadātaṃ karma cakṣuṣā, yadanivāritamenāṃ paśyati /

kuta ete rūpātiśayaparamāṇavaḥ samāsāditāḥ /

body.translated_text:
But his heart, having beheld the moonbeam-beauty of <s>Kādambarī's</s> face, surged up like the nectar of the ocean.
And there arose in his mind: 'Why did the Creator not make my remaining senses also consist entirely of eyes? Or what supremely meritorious deed has this eye performed, that it looks upon her without obstruction? Ah! This is a wondrous thing the Creator has produced — one single abode of all that is lovely! Whence has he procured these atoms of surpassing beauty? Surely, when the Creator was producing her, the teardrops that fell from his pair of eyes from the pain of stroking with his palms — from those have been born in this world the forests of night-lotuses, day-lotuses, blue lotuses, and fragrant water-lilies.'
Even as he was thinking thus, his gaze fell upon her pair of eyes. Then, as she too was thinking 'Surely this is the one whom <s>Keyūraka</s> announced,' her gaze — smiling with wonder at beholding such surpassing beauty, its target fixedly bound — fell upon him for a long time.
And <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, whitened by the radiance of her eyes, overwhelmed by the sight of <s>Kādambarī</s>, shone at that moment like an innocent boy.
And upon seeing him — first came horripilation, then the tinkling of ornaments, and thereupon <s>Kādambarī</s> rose to her feet.

madanaśaraprathamaprahāravedanaiva sītkarām <2> <2.śītkāram> akarot, kusumaprakaraketatīkaṇṭakakṣatiḥ sādhāraṇatāmavāpa /
vepathureva karatalamakampayat, nivedanodyatapratīhārīnivāraṇaṃ kapaṭamabhūt /
tadā ca kādambarīṃ viśato manmathasyāpi manmatha ivābhūd dvitīyaḥ, tayā saha yo viveśacandrāpīḍahṛdayam /
tathāhi, asāvapi tasyā ratnābharaṇadyutimāpa tirodhānamamasta, hṛdayapraveśamapi parigrahamagāṇayat, bhūṣaṇasvamapi sambhāṣaṇamamanyata, sarvendriyāharaṇamapi prasādamacintayat, dehaprabhāsamparkamapi suratasamāgamasukhamakalpayat /
body.translated_text:
Then it was the flower-armed one (<s>Kusumāyudha</s>, the God of Love) himself who produced her perspiration — the exertion of rising in haste became the pretext.
It was the trembling of the thighs itself that obstructed her gait — the flock of swans attracted by the sound of her anklets received the blame.
It was the flow of her sighs itself that made her garment flutter — the wind from the chowrie was assigned as the cause.
Her hand fell upon her heart, as if from eagerness to touch <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> who had entered within — that very gesture became the pretext of covering her breasts.
It was joy itself that let tears fall — the pollen from the flower dislodged from her ear-ornament became the pretext.
It was bashfulness itself that did not allow her to speak — the swarm of bees that had come drawn by the fragrance of her lotus-face served as the obstruction.
It was the pain of <s>Madana's</s> arrow's first strike itself that made her draw a hissing in-breath — the injury from the thorns of the <s>ketakī</s> in the flower-heap assumed common attribution.
It was trembling itself that shook her palm — the waving away of the doorkeeper who was about to make an announcement became the disguise.
And then, as <s>Manmatha</s> entered <s>Kādambarī</s>, there arose, as it were, a second <s>Manmatha</s> — who, together with her, entered <s>Candrāpīḍa's</s> heart.
For he too obtained the radiance of her gem ornaments and considered it concealment; he counted entering her heart as acceptance in marriage; he considered even the sound of ornaments as conversation; he thought of the captivation of all senses as a gracious favor; and he regarded the touch of her body's radiance as the pleasure of amorous union.

body.text:
kādambarī tu kṛcchrādiva dattakatipayapadā mahāśvetāṃ snehanirbharaṃ ciradarśanajātotkaṇṭhā <1> <1....jātotkaṇṭhaṃ> sotkaṇṭhaṃ kaṇṭhe jagrāha /
mahāśvetāpi dṛḍhataradattakaṇṭhagrahā tāmavādīt-"sakhi! kādambari! bhārate varṣe rājā aneka-vara-turaga-khura-mukhollekhadatta-catuḥ-mudra rakṣitaprajāpījastārāpīḍo nāma, tasyāyaṃ nija-bhuja-śilāstambha-viśrānta-viśva-viśvambharāpīḍaḥ <2> <2....viśrāntaviśvambharāpīḍaḥ, viśvabandhuḥ> candrāpīḍo nāma sūnudigvijayaprasaṅgenāgataḥ <3> <3.anugataḥ> bhūmimimām /
eṣa ca darśanāt prabhṛti prakṛtyā me niṣkāraṇabandhunāṃ gataḥ, parityaktasakalāsaṅganiṣṭhurāmapi me <4> <4.saviśeṣaiḥ> saviśeṣasvabhāvasaralairguṇairākuṣya <5> <5.ākramya> cittavṛttiṃ varttate, durllabho hi dākṣiṇyaparavaśo nirnimittamitramakṛtrimahṛdayo vidagdhajanaḥ <1> <1.vidagdho janaḥ> yato dṛṣṭavaivemam ahamiva tvamapi nirmāṇakauśalaṃ prajāpateḥ, niḥsapatnatāñca rūpasya, sthānābhinivaśitvañca lakṣmyāḥ, sadbharttṛtāsukhañca pṛthivyāḥ, suralokātiriktatāñca marttyalokasya, saphalatāñca mānuṣīlocanānām, ekasthānasamāgamñca sarvakalānāma, aiśvaryyañca saubhāgyasya, agrāmyatāñca manuṣyāṇāṃ jñāsyasīti balādānīto 'yam /
kathitā cāsya mayā bahuprakāraṃ <2> <2.bahukaraṃ> priyasakhī /
tadapūrvadarśano 'yamiti vimucya lajjām, anupajātaparicaya ityutsṛjya aviśrambhatām, avijñātaśīla ityapahāya śaṅkām, yathā mayi tathātrāpi varttitavyam <3> <3.pravarttitavyam> /
eṣa te mitrañca bāndhavaśca parijanaśca' ityāvedite tayā, candrāpīḍaḥ praṇāmamakarot /
kṛtapraṇāmañca taṃ tadā kādambaryyāstiryyagvilokayantyāḥ sasnehamatidīrghalocanāpāṅgabhāgaṃ gacchatastārakasya <1> <1.atidīrghalocanāyā apāṅgabhāgaṃ gacchatastārakasya locanasya atidīrghalocanayorapāṅgabhāgam> śrama-salila lava-visara ivānandabaṣpajabindunikaro nipapāta /
tvaritamabhiprasthitasya dhūliriva sudhādhavalā smitajyotsnā visasāra /
sammānyatāmayaṃ hṛdayaruciro janaḥ pratipraṇāmeneti śiro vaktumivaikā bhrūlatā samunnanāma /
aṅgulivivaraviniḥsṛtamarakatāṅgulīyakamayūkhalekho <2> <2....lekhābibhrama...aṅgulīyakalekhaḥ...> vibhrama-gṛhītatāmbūlavīṭika iva karo jṛmbhārambhamantharaṃ mukhamutasasarpa /
snavatsvedajaladhautalāvaṇyanirmmaleṣu cāsyāḥsaṃkrānta <1> <1.stambhasaṃkrānta...> -pratibimbatayā sañcaranmūrttirmakaraketurivāvayaveṣvadṛśyata candrāpīḍaḥ /
tathāhi, śiñjanmaṇinūpurapuṭena <2> <2....maṇikyanūpura> bhuvam <3> <3.maṇibhavam> ālikhatāṅguṣṭhenāhūta iva caraṇanakheṣu nipapāta /
darśanātirabhasapradhāvitena gatvā hṛdayenānīta-iva stanābhyantare sasadṛśyata /
vikacakuvalayadāmadīrghayā dṛṣṭyā ca nipīta iva kapolatale samalakṣyata /
sarvāsāmeva ca tadā tāsāṃ kanyakānāṃ tiryyak, paśyantīnāṃ taṃ kutūhalādapāṅgacumbinyo nirgantukāmā <4> <4.apāṅgacumbinyā daṣṭyā nirgantukāmā iva> iva karṇapūramadhukaraiḥ samaṃ babhrumustaralāstārakāḥ /
body.translated_text:
But <s>Kādambarī</s>, having with difficulty taken a few steps, overflowing with affection, longing from having not seen her for a long time, eagerly embraced <s>Mahāśvetā</s> around the neck.
<s>Mahāśvetā</s> too, holding her in a tighter embrace, spoke to her: 'Dear friend! <s>Kādambarī</s>! In the land of <s>Bhārata</s>, there is a king named <s>Tārāpīḍa</s>, whose subjects are protected, marked with the four seals imprinted by the hooves of his many excellent horses. His son, named <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, upon the stone pillars of whose arms the burden of the entire earth rests, has come to this land on the occasion of his conquest of the quarters.
And he, from the moment of seeing him, has become by nature one of my kinsmen without cause. Even though I have abandoned all attachments and am harsh, he continues to draw my mind's inclination by his virtues, which are especially genuine and straightforward by nature. For rare indeed is a refined person who is devoted to courtesy, whose friendship is without motive, and whose heart is genuine.
Therefore, upon seeing him, you too, like me, will appreciate the creative skill of <s>Prajāpati</s>, and the unrivalled nature of beauty, and the firm attachment of <s>Lakṣmī</s> to her abode, and the happiness of the earth in having a worthy lord, and the surpassing of the world of gods by the mortal world, and the fruitfulness of human eyes, and the congregation of all arts in one place, and the sovereignty of good fortune, and the refinement of human beings—you will come to know all this. Thus, he has been brought here forcibly.
And you have been spoken of to him by me in many ways as my dear friend. Therefore, letting go of shyness thinking "this is an unfamiliar sight," casting off distrust thinking "no acquaintance has yet arisen," removing apprehension thinking "his character is unknown"—as you behave toward me, so should you behave toward him too. He is your friend, and kinsman, and attendant.'
When she had thus announced this, <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> made a bow.
And as he bowed, from <s>Kādambarī</s> who was glancing sideways, as the pupil traveled lovingly to the far corner of her extremely long eyes, a shower of teardrops born of joy fell, like drops of perspiration from exertion.
The moonlight of her smile spread forth, white as lime-plaster, like the dust raised by one setting forth in haste.
As if to say 'Let this person who delights the heart be honored with a return-bow,' one creeper-like eyebrow rose upward.
Her hand, with rays of light streaming from an emerald ring through the gaps between her fingers—as if she had playfully taken a betel roll—slowly crept toward her mouth with the languidness of a beginning yawn.
And in her limbs, made pure by beauty washed with the water of bathing and perspiration, <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> appeared as a moving reflected figure, like <s>Makaraketu</s> (the God of Love) manifested in her body.
For, as if summoned by the great toe that scratched the ground within the cup of her tinkling jeweled anklet, he fell at her toenails.
As if carried there by a heart that rushed forth in the haste of seeing, he appeared within her breasts.
And as if drunk in by a gaze as long as a garland of blooming blue lotuses, he was perceived on the surface of her cheeks.
And of all those maidens then, looking at him sideways with curiosity, their restless pupils wandered together with the bees on their ear-ornaments, as if, kissing the corners of their eyes, they wished to fly out.

body.text:
kādambarī tu savibhrama-kṛta-prati-praṇāmā <5> <5....kṛtapraṇāmā> mahāśvetayā saha paryaṅke niṣasāda /
sasambhramaṃ <1> <1.sasambhramaparijanopanītāyāñca> parijanotāyāñca śayanaśirobhāganiveśitāyāṃ dhavalāṃśukapracchadapaṭāyāṃ <2> <2.atra vividharatnaprabhābhāsitāyām' iti kvacit pāṭho dṛśyate> hemapādāṅkitāyāṃ pīṭhikāyāṃ candrāpīḍaḥ samupāviśat /
mahāśvetānurodhena ca viditakādambarīcittābhiprāyāḥ saṃvṛta-mukha-nyasta-dattaśabda-nivāraṇa-saṃjñāḥ pratīhāryyo veṇuravān vīṇāghoṣāṃn gītadhvanīn māgadhījayaśabdāṃśca sarvato nivārayāñcakruḥ /
tvaritaparijanopanītena ca salilena kādambarī svayamutthāya mahāśvetāyāścaraṇau prakṣālyottarīyāṃśukenāpamṛjya punaḥ paryyaṅkamāruroha /
candrāpīḍasyāpi kādambaryyāḥ sakhī rūpānurūpā jīvitanirviśeṣā sarvaviśrambhabhūmirmadalekheti nāmnā balādanicchato 'pi prakṣālitavatī caraṇau /
mahāsvetā tu karṇābharaṇaprabhāvaṣiṇyaṃsadeśe <3> <3....apāṅgadeśe> saprema-pāṇinā spṛśantī, madhukarabhara-paryyastañca karṇāvataṃsasamutkṣipantī, cāmarapavanavidhuti <4> <4....vidhūti...> paryyastāñca <5> <5....paryyattālaka...> alakavallarīmanuṣvajamānā kādambarīmanāmayaṃ papraccha /
sā tu sakhīpremṇā gṛhanivāsena kṛtāparādhevānāmayenaiva lajjamānā kṛcchrādiva kuśalamācacakṣe /
samupajātaśokāpi ca tasmin kāle <1> <1.iha "tasmin kāle' iti kvacitpustake nāvalokyate> mahāśvetāmukhanirīkṣaṇatatparāpi muhurmuhurapāṅga-vikṣepa-pracalita-tarala-tara-tāraśārodaraṃ <2> <2....sārodaraṃ> cakṣurmaṇḍalitacāpena bhagavatā kusumadhanvanā balānnīyamānaṃ candrāpīḍapīḍanāyeva <3> <3....pīḍanayeva, candrāpīḍapīḍanādeva, candrāpīḍaṃ prati> na śaśāka nivārayitum /
tenaiva kṣaṇena tenāsannasakhokapolasaṃkrāntenerṣyām <4> <4.irṣyayār irṣyā> , romāñca-bhidyamāna-kucataṭa <5> <5.kvacit "taṭa' iti padaṃ nopalabhyate> -naśayat-pratibimbena virahavyathām, svedārdra <6> <6.virahavyathāsvedārdra...> -vakṣaḥsthala ghaṭitaśālabhañjikāpratimena sapatnīroṣaṃ <1> <1.sapatnīroṣāt> nimiṣatā daurbhāgyaśokam, ānandajalatirohitenāndhatāduḥkhamabhajata sā /
muhūrttāpagame ca tāmbūladānodyatāṃ mahāśvetā tāmabhāṣata <2> <2.tāṃ mahāśvetāṃ samabhāṣata> -ṭhasakhi! kādambari! sampratipannameva <3> <3.kvacideva pāṭho nāsti> sarvābhirevāsmābhiḥ <4> <4.sarvābhirasmābhiḥ, sarvābhirevāsmābhirabhinava...> ayamabhinavāgataścandrāpīḍa ārādhanīyaḥ, tadasmai tāvaddoyatāṃ tāmbūlam <5> <5.kvacit "tāmbūlam' iti padaṃ na dṛśyate> ' ityuktā ca kiñcidvivarttitāvanamitamukhī <6> <6....ānamitamukhī> śanairavyaktamiva "priyasakhi! lajje 'hamanupajāparicayā prāgalbhyenānena, gṛhāṇa, tvamevāsmai prayaccha' ityuvāca <7> <7.sā tām> /
punaḥ <8> <8.kādambarī tu> punarabhidhīyamānā ca tayā kathamapi gramyeva cirāddānābhimukhaṃ <9> <9.cireṇa> manuścakre /
mahāśvetāmukhādanākṛṣṭadṛṣṭireva <10> <10.anākarṣitadṛṣṭireva> vepamānāṅgayaṣṭirākulalocanā <11> <11.āmukulitalocanā, ākulitalocanā> sthūlasthūlaṃ niśvasatī <12> <12.niḥśvasantī> nijaśaraprahāramūcchitā manmathena snapiteva svedajalavisaraiḥ, svedajalavisaranimajjanabhayena ca hastāvalambanamiva yācamānā, sādhvasaparavaśā patāmīti lagitumiva <1> <1.vilagitubhiva, lapitumiva, tāpitumiva> kṛtaprayatnā prasārayāmāsa tāmbūlagarbha hastapallavam /
candrāpīḍastu jayakuñjarakumbhasthalāsphālana-saṃkrānta siṃdūramiva svabhāvapāṭalaṃ, dhanurguṇakarṣaṇakṛtakiṇaśyāmalam, kacagrahākṛṣṭi-ruditārilakṣmī-locana-parāmarśa-lagnāñjanabindumiva, visarpannakhakiraṇatayā atirabhasena pradhāvitābhirivaṃ vivardhitābhiriva prahasitābhirivāṅgulībhirupetam, sparśalobhācca tatkālakṛta-sanniveśāḥ sarāgāḥ pañcāpīndriyavṛttīraparā ivāṅgulīrudvahantam <3> <3.aparāṅgulīḥ,...vṛttīrivāṅgulīḥ...> prasāritavān pāṇim /
tatra ca sā tatkāla-sulabha <1> <1.kvacit "sulabha' iti padaṃ nāsti> -vilāsa-darśana-kuhūhalibhiriva kuto 'pyāgatya sarvarasairadhiṣṭhitā <2> <2....adhiṣṭhitenānyanibaddhalākṣyaśūnya...> /
tenānibaddhalakṣyatā śūnyaprasāritena, candrāpīḍahastānveṣaṇāyeva puraḥpravarttita-nakhāṃśunivahena, vepathucalitavalayāvalīvācālena sambhāṣaṇamiva kurvatā hastena, svedasalilapātapūrvakaṃ "gṛhyatāmayaṃ manmathena datto dāsajanaḥ' ityātmānamiva pratigrāhayantī, "adya prabhṛti bhavato haste varttate' iti jīvitamiva sthāpayantī, tāmbūlamadāt /
ākarṣantī <3> <3.ākarṣayantī> ca karakisalayaṃ bhujalatānusāreṇa sparśatṛṣṇāgatamanaṅgaśarabhinnamadhyaṃ hṛdayamiva patitamapi ratnavalayaṃ nājñāsīt /
gṛhītvā cāparaṃ tāmbūlaṃ mahāśvetāyai prāyacchat /
body.translated_text:
But <s>Kādambarī</s>, having made a return-bow in a flurried manner, sat upon the couch together with <s>Mahāśvetā</s>.
And on a seat with golden feet, covered with a white silk cloth, hurriedly brought by attendants and placed at the head of the bed, <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> sat down.
At <s>Mahāśvetā's</s> urging, the doorkeepers, who understood the intention of <s>Kādambarī's</s> heart, with closed mouths giving signals to stop the sounds, silenced everywhere the sounds of flutes, the resonance of <s>vīṇās</s>, the strains of songs, and the proclamations of bards.
And with water quickly brought by attendants, <s>Kādambarī</s> herself rose, washed <s>Mahāśvetā's</s> feet and wiped them with the edge of her upper garment, and again ascended to the couch.
<s>Kādambarī's</s> friend too — matching her in beauty, inseparable from her life, the ground of all her confidence, named <s>Madalekhā</s> — forcibly washed the feet of even the unwilling <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>.
And <s>Mahāśvetā</s>, lovingly touching with her hand <s>Kādambarī's</s> shoulder-region where the radiance of ear-ornaments rained, lifting up the ear-ornament that had been overturned by the weight of bees, and smoothing back the creeper-like locks tossed by the wind of the chowrie, asked <s>Kādambarī</s> about her well-being.
But she, as if feeling guilty toward her friend's love for having stayed at home, embarrassed even by the inquiry about her well-being, with difficulty as it were reported that she was well.
And though grief arose in her at that time, and though she was intent on gazing at <s>Mahāśvetā's</s> face, her eye — whose extremely restless pupil was set in motion by repeated sidelong glances, being forcibly drawn by the blessed <s>Kusumadhanvan</s> (the flower-bowed god of love) who had curved his bow, as if for the tormenting of <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> — she was unable to restrain.
In that very instant, from that reflection of his that had transferred to the cheek of her nearby friend, she experienced jealousy; from the reflection vanishing on the breast-surface being split by horripilation, the pain of separation; from the image resembling a <s>śālabhañjikā</s> statue fitted to the perspiration-moist chest-surface, the anger toward a co-wife; from blinking, the grief of misfortune; and from the reflection being hidden by tears of joy, the sorrow of blindness — all these she experienced.
And after a moment, <s>Mahāśvetā</s> addressed her who was ready to offer betel: 'O friend! <s>Kādambarī</s>! It has been agreed by all of us that this newly arrived <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> is to be honored; therefore, let betel be given to him first.'
And when thus spoken to, with her face slightly turned and bowed, softly and indistinctly as it were, she said: 'Dear friend! I am bashful, having no familiarity that has arisen for such boldness. Take it — you yourself give it to him.'
But being urged again and again by her, with great difficulty, like a rustic, she at length brought her mind to the act of giving.
With her gaze not drawn from <s>Mahāśvetā's</s> face, with her limb-staff trembling, her eyes agitated, sighing heavily, as if swooned from the strike of his own arrow, as if bathed by <s>Manmatha</s> with floods of perspiration-water, as if begging for the support of a hand from fear of drowning in the flood of perspiration, overcome by timidity, making efforts as if trying to catch herself from falling — she extended her sprout-like hand containing the betel.
And <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, with a hand naturally rosy like vermilion transferred from the striking of the frontal-globe of the elephant of victory, darkened with calluses from drawing the bowstring, as if spotted with collyrium-drops from the touch of the weeping eyes of the <s>Lakṣmī</s> of the enemy whose hair was grasped, endowed with fingers that, by the spreading of their nail-rays, seemed to be running forth swiftly, seemed to be growing, seemed to be laughing aloud — and bearing what seemed like additional fingers, being the passionate dispositions of the five senses arranged at that moment from eagerness for touch — extended his palm.
And there she was as if possessed by all the <s>rasas</s> (sentiments) that had come from somewhere, as if curious to witness the coquetry readily available at that moment. With that hand extended emptily without a fixed target, with streams of nail-rays advancing before it as if searching for <s>Candrāpīḍa's</s> hand, with a hand that seemed to be making conversation through its row of bangles set chattering by trembling, preceded by the fall of perspiration-water — as if offering herself saying 'Accept this servant given by <s>Manmatha</s>,' as if entrusting her life saying 'From today onward it rests in your hand' — she gave the betel.
And drawing back her sprout-like hand along the course of her vine-like arm, she did not even notice the gem bracelet that had fallen — like a heart pierced through the middle by <s>Anaṅga's</s> arrow, arising from the thirst for touch.
And taking another betel, she offered it to <s>Mahāśvetā</s>.

body.text:
atha sahasaiva tvaritagatiḥ, trivarṇarāgamindrāyudhamiva kuṇḍalīkṛtaṃ kaṇṭhena vahatā vidrumāṅkurānukāricañcupuṭena <1> <1....anukāriṇā cañcupuṭena> marakatadyutipakṣatinā mantharagatena śukenānubadhyamānā, <2> <2.mandharagamanena śukenānugamyamānā> kumuda-kesarapiñjaratayā caraṇayugalasya, campakakalikākāratayā ca mukhasya, kuvalayadalanīlatayā ca pakṣadyutīnām, kusumamayīvāgatya sārikā sakrodhamavādīt-bharttṛdārike! kādambari! kasmānna nivārayasyenamalīkasubhagābhimāninamatiduvinītaṃ <3> <3.durvinītaṃ> māmanuvadhnantaṃ vihaṅgāpasadam <4> <4.vihaṅgamāpasadam> /
yadi māmanena paribhūyamānāmupekṣase tato 'haṃ niyatamātmānamutsṛjāmi /
satyaṃ śapāmi te pādapaṅkajasparśena' ityevamabhihitā ca tayā kādambarī smitamakarot /
aviditavṛttāntā tu mahāśvetā"kimiyaṃ vadati' iti madalekhāṃ papraccha /
sā <5> <5.tvakaḥ> cākathayat-"eṣā bhartṛduhituḥ sakhī <6> <6.kvacit sakhīti padaṃ na dṛśyate> kādambaryyāḥ kālindīti nāmnā sārikā, etasya <1> <1.idamasya ca> parihāsanāmnaḥ śuksaya bharttṛdārikayaiva pāṇigrahaṇapūrvakaṃ jāyāpadaṃ grāhitā /
adya cāyamanayā pratyuṣasi kādambaryyāstāmbūlakaraṅkavāhinīmimāṃ tamālikāmekākinīṃ <2> <2.taralikā...> kimapi pāṭhayan dṛṣṭo yataḥ, tataḥ prabhṛti sañjāterṣyā kopaparāṅmukhī nainamupasarpati, nālapati, na spṛśati, na vilokayati, sarvābhirasmābhiḥ prasādyamānāpi na prasīdatī'ti <3> <3.kvacit "iti' iti padaṃ nāvalokyate> /
etadākarṇya sphuritakapolodaraścandrāpīḍo mandaṃ mandaṃ vihasyābravīt-"astyeṣā kathā, śrūyata evaitadrājakule karṇaparamparayā, parijano 'pyevaṃ mantrayate, <4> <4.āmantrayate, apyevaṃ mantrayati evam, api mantrayate> bahirapi janāḥ kathayanti, evaṃ digantareṣvapyayamālāpo varttata eva <5> <5.evam> , asmābhirapyetadākarṇitameva, "yathā kila devyāḥ kādambaryyāstāgbūladāyinī <6> <6.vāhinīṃ> tamālikāṃ <7> <7.taralikāṃ> kāmayamānaḥ parityaktanijakalatro nistrapayā <8> <8.nistrapaḥ> anayā saha, devyāstu kādambaryyāḥ kathametad yuktaṃ yanna nivārayatīmāṃ capalāṃ duṣṭadāsīm /
athavā devyāpi kathitaiva niḥsnehatā <1> <1.nisnehatā> prathamameva varākīmimāṃ kālindīmīdṛśāya durvinītāya vihaṅgāya prayacchantyā kimidānīmiyaṃ <2> <2.kvacidiha"tapasvino' ityadhika pāṭhaḥ samupalabhyate> karotu, yadetat sāpatnyakaraṇaṃnīrīṇāṃ pradhānaṃ kopakāraṇam, agraṇīrvirāgahetuḥ, paraṃ paribhasthānam /
iyameva kevalamatidhīrā, yadanayānena daurbhāgyagārimṇā jātavairāgyayā viṣaṃ vā nāsvāditam, analo vā nāsāditaḥ anaśanaṃ vā nāṅgīkṛtam /
na hyevaṃvigham <3> <3.na hyekam> aparamasti yoṣitāṃ laghimnaḥ kāraṇam /
yadi ceyamīdṛśe 'pyaparādhe anunīyamānā <4> <4.abhibhavanirāsyām, abhibhavanirasyā> anena pratyāsattimeṣyati /
tadā dhigimām alamanayā, dūrato varjanīyeyam, abhibhavanirāsyā <5> <5.abhibhavanirāsyām, abhibhavanirasyā> , /
ka enāṃ punarālāpayiṣyati, ko vāvalokayiṣyati, ko vāsyā nāma grahīṣyati' ityevamabhihitavati tasmin sarvāstāḥ saha kādambaryyāḥ krīḍālāpabhāvitāḥ <6> <6....bhāṣitāḥ> jahasuraṅganāḥ /
parihāsastu tasya narmmabhāṣitamākarṇya jagāda-dhūrtte! rājaputra! nipuṇeyam, na tvayānyena vā lolāpi pratārayituṃ śakyate /
eṣāpi budhyata evaitāvatīrvakroktīḥ, iyamapi jānātyeva parihāsajalpitāni, asyā api rājakulasamparkacaturāmatiḥ /
viramyatām, abhūmireṣā bhujaṅga-bhaṅgi-bhāṣitānām, iyameva hi vetti mañjubhāṣiṇī kālañca kāraṇañca pramāṇañca viṣayca prastāvañca kopaprasādayoḥ iti /
body.translated_text:
Then, suddenly, with swift gait — being followed by a slow-gaited parrot that bore on its neck what seemed like a rainbow of three colors coiled up, with a beak-cup imitating coral sprouts, and wings of emerald luster — a <s>sārikā</s> (myna bird), as if made entirely of flowers, with the yellowness of night-lotus filaments in its pair of feet, the form of a <s>campaka</s> bud in its face, and the blueness of blue-lotus petals in the radiance of its wings, came forward and spoke angrily:
'O master's daughter! <s>Kādambarī</s>! Why do you not restrain this falsely self-conceited, utterly ill-mannered low-born bird that follows me? If you disregard me being insulted by this one, then I shall certainly give up my life. I swear truly by the touch of your lotus-feet!'
And when thus addressed by her, <s>Kādambarī</s> smiled.
But <s>Mahāśvetā</s>, not knowing the circumstances, asked <s>Madalekhā</s>, 'What is she saying?'
And she explained: 'This is a <s>sārikā</s> bird named <s>Kālindī</s>, a friend of our master's daughter <s>Kādambarī</s>. She was given the status of wife to this parrot — whose very name is a jest — by the master's daughter herself through a formal marriage ceremony. And today, this one was seen by her at dawn privately teaching something to <s>Tamālikā</s>, <s>Kādambarī's</s> betel-box carrier, when she was alone. Since then, with jealousy aroused, turning away in anger, she does not approach him, does not speak to him, does not touch him, does not look at him. Even though being placated by all of us, she is not appeased.'
Hearing this, <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, with cheeks quivering, gently laughing, said: 'This tale exists indeed; it is heard in the royal household by word of mouth. Even the attendants discuss it thus; even outsiders tell of it. Even in distant regions this talk goes on. Even we have heard this — that indeed, desiring <s>Tamālikā</s>, the betel-bearer of the Lady <s>Kādambarī</s>, having abandoned his own wife, shamelessly with her... But how is it proper of the Lady <s>Kādambarī</s> that she does not restrain this fickle, wicked maidservant? Or rather, even the Lady's heartlessness has been made evident in giving this poor <s>Kālindī</s> at the very first to such an ill-mannered bird. What should she do now, when this creating of a co-wife is the chief cause of women's anger, the foremost cause of estrangement, the supreme occasion for humiliation? She alone is exceedingly patient — that, having been disgusted with this wretch of ill-fortune, she has neither tasted poison, nor sought fire, nor undertaken a fast unto death. For there is no other such cause for a woman's dishonor. And if she, even after such an offense, being conciliated, will come close to him again — then shame on her! Enough of her! She should be avoided from afar, she should be discarded. Who would ever speak to her again? Who would even look at her? Who would even take her name?'
And when he had spoken thus, all those women, along with <s>Kādambarī</s>, recognizing it as playful conversation, laughed.
But the jester, hearing his witty speech, said: 'O rogue! O prince! This one is clever — even being fickle, she cannot be deceived by you or by anyone else. She too understands this many indirect speeches; she too knows well the talk of jest; her mind too is clever from association with the royal household. Desist! This one is not the ground for serpentine speech. For she herself, the sweet-speaking one, knows the time, the cause, the measure, the scope, and the occasion of both anger and grace.'

body.translated_text:
In the meanwhile, a chamberlain (<s>kañcukī</s>) came and addressed <s>Mahāśvetā</s>: "O long-lived one! King <s>Citraratha</s> and Queen <s>Madirā</s> summon you to see them."
Being thus addressed and wishing to go, she asked <s>Kādambarī</s>: "Friend! Where should <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> stay?"
She, however, laughing inwardly — thinking "Is it not sufficient that he has resided in the hearts of countless women?" — spoke aloud: "Friend <s>Mahāśvetā</s>! Why do you say such a thing? From the very first sight, he is indeed the master even of my body, how much more so of my mansion, wealth, or attendants! Wherever it pleases him, or the heart of my dear friend, let him stay there."
Hearing that, <s>Mahāśvetā</s> said: "Right here, in the pleasure garden near your palace, let him stay in the jeweled mansion on the pleasure-hill" — and having said this, she went to see the <s>Gandharva</s> king.

body.translated_text:
And <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> too, going out together with her for amusement, followed by maidens sent by the chief doorkeeper as directed by <s>Kādambarī</s> — <s>vīṇā</s>-players, those skilled in flute-playing, those accomplished in the art of song, those fond of dice games, those clever at the game of <s>aṣṭāpada</s> (chess), those who had labored at the art of painting, and reciters of fine sayings — with <s>Keyūraka</s>, who had seen the place before, showing him the way, he went to the gem-pavilion on the pleasure-hill.
When he had gone, the <s>Gandharva</s> king's daughter, having dismissed all her friends and attendants, followed by only a limited number of maidservants, ascended to her upper palace.
There, falling upon her bed, though attended by maidservants standing at a distance, modest and restrained in conduct, her consciousness somehow having returned from somewhere, alone at that time — as if restrained by shame saying 'O fickle one! What is this you have begun!'; as if reproached by modesty saying 'O daughter of the <s>Gandharva</s> king! How is this proper?'; as if mocked by innocence saying 'Where has that unsophisticated childishness of yours gone?'; as if addressed by maidenly modesty saying 'O wanton one! Do not practice immodesty as you please when alone!'; as if censured by dignity saying 'O timid one! This is not the way of maidens of noble family!'; as if threatened by decorum saying 'O ill-mannered one! Guard your modesty!'; as if instructed by noble birth saying 'O fool! You have been brought to disgrace by <s>Madana</s> (Love)!'; as if condemned by fortitude saying 'Whence comes this fickleness of heart in you?'; as if blamed by family honor saying 'O willful one! You have disregarded me!' — she bore an exceedingly heavy burden of shame.
And she thought thus: 'Heedless of all suspicion, displaying fickleness of heart — what have I, blinded by delusion, done today? For indeed, being reckless, I did not consider that this person had never been seen before. Being shameless, I did not reckon that the world would deem me fickle-hearted. Being foolish, I did not examine what his disposition might be. Being restless, I did not deliberate whether I might not even be pleasing to his sight. I was not afraid of the embarrassment of rejection; I was not fearful of elders; I was not troubled by public reproach. And that <s>Mahāśvetā</s> is greatly distressed — this I callously disregarded. That even friends standing nearby would observe — this I dully failed to notice. That attendants standing beside me would see — this I, who had lost all sense, did not perceive.
Even dull-witted people would discern such a lapse of propriety — how much more so <s>Mahāśvetā</s>, who has experienced the course of love; or friends skilled in all arts; or attendants adept in court ways who always understand the meaning of gestures! In such matters, the harem maidservants have exceedingly keen sight.
In every way I am ruined, wretched in merit! Death would be better for me today — not this shameful life. What will my mother say upon hearing this tale? Or my father? Or the <s>Gandharva</s> world? What shall I do? What remedy is there? By what means can I conceal this stumble? Or to whom shall I speak of this fickleness of these unruly senses? Or where shall I go, seized by the five-arrowed one (<s>Pañcabāṇa</s>) who has burned my heart?
Moreover, a promise was made through <s>Mahāśvetā's</s> intervention; it was declared before dear friends; and a message was entrusted to <s>Keyūraka's</s> hands. I, the unfortunate one, truly do not know whether by treacherous fate, or by overwhelming love, or by the accumulated demerit of former deeds, or by the destructiveness of death, or by some other agency, this deceiver <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> has been brought to me. Or some person who was never before seen, nor experienced, nor heard of, nor thought of, nor imagined, has come to torment me — by the mere sight of whom my senses have been, as it were, bound and surrendered; by <s>Manmatha</s> (the God of Love), as it were, placed in a cage of arrows and handed over; by passion, as it were, made a slave-woman and led away; by my heart, as it were, sold with virtues taken as the price — I have become utterly subject to him.'
'I shall have nothing to do with that fickle one' — she resolved for but a moment.
But having made that resolve, she was mocked, as it were, by <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> within her heart, who trembled with the heart's agitation, saying 'O falsely modest one! If you want nothing to do with me — here, I depart!'; and questioned, as it were, by her life-breath clinging to her throat, setting forth at the very moment of the resolve to abandon him; and addressed, as it were, by tears that arrived at that very moment, saying 'O you who know no distinctions! Look once more with washed eyes and see whether that person is worthy of rejection or not!'; and threatened, as it were, by the god of love saying 'I shall strip from you by force the pride of fortitude!' — once again, her heart turned toward <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> just as before.
Then, with the strength of her counter-resolve exhausted, rendered powerless by the onset of love, rising up as if helpless, she stood at the lattice window gazing at that very pleasure-hill.
And standing there, as if distressed by the obstruction of a flood of joy, she saw him with memory, not with her eyes. As if afraid of the touch of sweat dripping from her fingers, she painted him with thought, not with a brush. As if apprehensive of concealment by horripilation, she embraced him with her heart, not with her bosom. As if unable to bear the delay of the time of union with him, she employed her mind for going and coming, not her attendants.
And <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> too, entering freely what seemed like a second gem-pavilion that was <s>Kādambarī's</s> heart, falling upon a coverlet spread on a stone surface with many cushions placed one above another on both sides, his pair of feet held in <s>Keyūraka's</s> lap, surrounded by those maidens stationed at their assigned places — with his mind wavering, he entered into contemplation:
'Are these enchanting gestures of this daughter of the <s>Gandharva</s> king, <s>Kādambarī</s>, which captivate the hearts of all people, simply natural to her? Or have they been directed at me by the blessed <s>Makaraketu</s> (the God of Love), who is gracious without being propitiated — so that she glances at me sideways with eyes tearful, passionate, narrowed to a third of their width, as if reddened by the pollen-dust of <s>Smara's</s> flower-arrows falling within the heart?
And when caught looking at me, she covers herself with modesty, as if with a veil of the white light of her smile. And when her face turns from shyness of me, she offers the mirror of her cheek, as if covetous that my reflection might enter it. With her fingernail she traces upon the bed what seems like the first line of passion of a heart that gives me an opening. With her palm — from which a cluster of bees buzzing about a red lotus has been shaken off by the exertion of bringing me a betel offering — she fans her perspiring face, as if she had taken a <s>tamāla</s> leaf-fan.'
And again he thought: 'Probably it is the fickleness common to mortals that deceives me thus with thousands of false imaginings; or the intoxication of youth, bereft of discernment, intoxicates me — or <s>Madana</s> (Love) himself. For the sight of young men, as if afflicted by darkness, sees even a small stain as great. Even a particle of affection is amplified far by the intoxication of youth. Restlessness, agitated by hundreds of anxieties of its own creation, imagines everything — like a poet's fancy that is not at peace. The young mind's disposition, seized by skillful <s>Manmatha</s>, does not fail to paint something — like a brush held in expert hands. Self-conceit, having developed pride in one's own beauty, does not fail to offer itself somewhere — like a wanton woman. Desire shows even what has not been experienced — like a dream. Hope places before one even what is impossible — like a magical fan of illusion.'
And further he thought: 'What is the use of tormenting one's mind in vain? If this bright-eyed one has truly developed such a disposition toward me, then before long, <s>Manmatha</s> himself, favorable even without being entreated, will make it manifest. He himself will be the cutter of this doubt.'
Having thus determined, rising and sitting up, with those maidens he passed the time playing with dice, songs, <s>vīṇā</s>-music, hand-drums, debates on musical notes, conversations about fine sayings, and other such delicate artistic pastimes.
And having stayed a short while, going out, his mind drawn by curiosity to see the garden, he ascended to the peak of the pleasure-hill.

body.text:
kādambarī tu taṃ <5> <5.tātaṃ> dṛṣṭvā cirayatīti mahāśvetāyāḥ kila vartmāvalokayituṃ <6> <6.kvacidiha "udyatā' ityadhikaḥ pāṭhaḥ> vimucya taṃ gavākṣam <7> <7.vimucyatāṃ gavākṣamityuktvā> anaṅgakṣiptacittā saudhasyoparitanaṃ śikharamāruroha <8> <8.talaṃ kailāśaśikharamiva gauryaruroha> /
tatra ca viralaparijanā sakala <9> <9.kvacit, "sakala' padaṃ na dṛśyate> śaśimaṇḍalapāṇḍureṇātapatreṇa hemadaṇḍena <1> <1.viracitahemadaṇḍena> nivāryamāṇātapā, caturbhirbālavyajanaiśca phenaśucibhiruddhūyamānairupavījyamānā, śirasi, kusumagandhalubdhena bhramatā bhramarakulena divāpi nīlāvaguṇṭhaneneva <2> <2.nīlāvaguṇṭhaneva> candrāpīḍabhisaraṇaveśābhyāsamiva kurvatī <3> <3....veṣābhyasyantī,...veśābhyāsaṃ kurvatī, kailāsaśikhara iva gaurī ityapi kvacidadhikaḥ pāṭhaḥ> , muhuścāmaraśikhāṃ samāsajya, muhuśchatradaṇḍamavalambya, muhustamālikāskandhe karau vinyasya, muhurmadalekhāṃ pariṣvajya <4> <4....sakhī pariṣvajya> muhuḥ parijanāntaritasakaladehā netratribhāgeṇa <5> <5....netratribhāgeṇāvalokya> , muhurāvalitatrivalīvalayā parivṛtya, muhuḥ pratīhārīvetralatāśikhare kapolaṃ nidhāya, muhurniścalakaravidhṛtāmadharapallave vīṭikāṃ viniveśya <6> <6.niveśya> , muhurudgīrṇotpalaprahāra <7> <7.udgūrṇakarṇotpala...udgīrṇakarṇotpala> -palāyamāna-parijanānusaraṇa-datta-katipayapadā vihasya, taṃ vilokayantī tena ca vilokyamānā, mahāntamapi kālamatikrāntaṃ nājñāsīt /
āruhya ca pratīhāryā niveditamahāśvetāpratyāgamanā tasmādavatatāra /
snānādiṣu mandādarāpi mahāśvetānurodhena divasavyāpāramakarot /
candrāpīḍo 'pi tasmādavatīrya prathamavisarjitenaiva kādambarīparijanena nirvarttitasnānavidhirnirupahata <1> <1.nivarttita...> -śilātalāccitābhimatadaivataḥ <2> <2....śilārccita...> krīḍāparyataka eva sarvamāhārādikamahaḥkarma cakre /
body.translated_text:
<s>Kādambarī</s>, having seen him (her father), and thinking that <s>Mahāśvetā</s> was taking long, left that window to look at the road for her return; her mind agitated by <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless god of love), she ascended to the upper pinnacle of the palace.
There, with few attendants around her, the sunlight being warded off by a parasol white as the full moon's orb with a golden handle, being fanned by four small fans white as foam that were being waved about, on her head a swarm of bees hovering about greedy for the fragrance of flowers forming even during the day what seemed like a dark veil, as if she were rehearsing the costume for a secret rendezvous with <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> — now touching the tip of a <s>cāmara</s> (yak-tail fan), now leaning on the parasol handle, now placing her hands on <s>Tamālikā's</s> shoulder, now embracing <s>Madalekhā</s>, now with her whole body screened by attendants gazing with a mere third part of her eye, now turning around with the coils of her triple-folded waist visible, now resting her cheek on the tip of the doorkeeper's cane, now placing a <s>vīṭikā</s> (betel roll) held in a motionless hand upon her lower lip, now laughing and taking a few steps chasing the attendants who fled from being struck with a flung lotus — gazing at him and being gazed at by him, she did not realize that even a great span of time had passed.
Having gone up, when the doorkeeper informed her that <s>Mahāśvetā</s> had not returned, she descended from there.
Though with little interest in bathing and the like, out of regard for <s>Mahāśvetā</s> she carried on the daily routine.
<s>Candrāpīḍa</s> too, having descended from there, his bathing ritual completed by the very attendants of <s>Kādambarī</s> who had been sent to him earlier, having worshipped his chosen deities on an unblemished stone surface, performed all daily duties such as eating right there in the pleasure garden.
