Then, interrupting the words of him who spoke thus, <s>Madalekhā</s> said with a smile: "O prince! Enough, by excessive restraint my friend <s>Kādambarī</s> is distressed. Why is such a thing even said? All this has been accepted by her even without words; why then is she placed on the swing of doubt by these trifling courtesies of speech?"
And having stayed for some time, making conversation, she asked everything: "How is King <s>Tārāpīḍa</s>? How is Queen <s>Vilāsavatī</s>? How is the venerable <s>Śukanāsa</s>? What is <s>Ujjayinī</s> like? How far away is it? What is the land of <s>Bhārata</s> like? Is the mortal world delightful?"
Having remained for a long time with such and other conversations, <s>Kādambarī</s> rose and instructed <s>Keyūraka</s> to sleep near <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, and the attendants too, and ascended to the pinnacle of the sleeping palace.
There she prepared a bed spread with a canopy of white silk.
<s>Candrāpīḍa</s> too, on that very stone terrace, contemplating in his mind the absence of pride, the beauty, and the profound depth of <s>Kādambarī</s>, the causeless affection of <s>Mahāśvetā</s>, the goodness of <s>Madalekhā</s>, the greatness of the attendants, the exceeding prosperity of the <s>Gandharva</s> king's realm, and the loveliness of the <s>Kimpuruṣa</s> country — with his feet being massaged by <s>Keyūraka</s> — passed the night as if in an instant.
Then gradually, the lord of stars (the moon), wearied by wakefulness from beholding <s>Kādambarī</s>, descended as if to sleep into the row of shore-groves of <s>tāla</s>, <s>tamāla</s>, <s>tālī</s>, and plantain trees, cooled by the sparse breeze of waves.
And the moonlight grew wan, as if by the hot sighs of the lovelorn women nearby.
Like <s>Lakṣmī</s> (splendor) of the night, aroused by love from beholding <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, carried in the bosom of <s>kumuda</s> (water-lily) petals, she fell upon the lotuses.
And at the departure of night — as the lamps in the bedchambers grew pale and thin, as if yearning, remembering the blows of women's ear-lotuses; as the dawn breezes blew carrying the fragrance of tree-creeper blossoms, whirling as if with the sighs of the love-god wearied by incessant arrow-shooting; as the stars became dimmed by the rising of dawn, as if in fear seeking refuge in the bower-houses of <s>Mandara</s> mountain creepers; and as the sun gradually rose, bearing a disk reddish as if stained with the love dwelling in the hearts of <s>cakravāka</s> birds — <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> arose from the stone terrace, washed his lotus-face, performed the salutation to <s>Sandhyā</s> (twilight), took <s>tāmbūla</s> (betel), and said: "<s>Keyūraka</s>! Go and see whether the princess <s>Kādambarī</s> is awake or not, and where she is."
And when <s>Keyūraka</s> went and returned, reporting "She is on the terrace of the courtyard at the base of the <s>Mandara</s> palace, together with <s>Mahāśvetā</s>," he came to see the <s>Gandharva</s> king's daughter.
And he saw <s>Mahāśvetā</s>, who was receiving elderly relatives of the <s>Gandharva</s> king who had come to visit — greeting them respectfully with salutations, addresses, risings, and offerings of nearby cane-seats — surrounded by female ascetics with white ash marks on their foreheads, with palms moving from turning rosaries, following the <s>Pāśupata</s> vow and wearing robes reddened with mineral dyes; by wandering mendicant women; by those bearing the vow of red cloth in garments reddened like ripe palm-fruit bark; by those with white cloth tightly binding breast-coverings identified as white-cloth devotees; by female ascetics bearing matted hair, animal skins, <s>muñja</s> grass girdles, bark garments, and <s>āṣāḍha</s> staffs as marks of their order — as if by the very deities of sacred <s>mantras</s> — who were reciting the holy hymns of Lord <s>Tryambaka</s> (Śiva), <s>Ambikā</s>, <s>Kārttikeya</s>, <s>Viṣṭaraśravas</s> (Kubera), <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>, the noble <s>Avalokiteśvara</s>, the <s>Arhat</s>, and <s>Viriñca</s> (Brahmā), who was being worshipped. She was also receiving with honor, through salutations, conversations, risings, and offerings of nearby seats, elderly relatives of the <s>Gandharva</s> king who had come to see her, through the inner apartments. And she was giving her attention as a daughter of <s>Nārada</s>, singing in a sweet voice while a <s>Kinnara</s> couple seated behind played a melody on two sweet bamboo flutes, set the beat, and while the great and auspicious <s>Mahābhārata</s> was being recited. And before a gem-mirror held up, she was gazing at her reflection — the interior darkened by the blackness produced by the thick redness of <s>tāmbūla</s> (betel) stain, her lower lip pinkened like a polished beeswax tablet sprinkled with the lustre of her teeth's moonlight. And he saw <s>Kādambarī</s> too, upon whom a household <s>haṃsa</s> (swan), with eyes turned upward, drawn by desire for <s>śaivala</s> (moss), sent forth from the <s>śirīṣa</s> flower ear-ornament, was circling as if performing the salutation, circumambulation, and bow of the dawn moon.
Approaching and making his bow, he took a seat placed on that very limestone terrace.
And having stayed for some time, looking at <s>Mahāśvetā's</s> face, he made a gentle smile with the inner surface of his cheeks quivering.
She, understanding his intent from just that, said to <s>Kādambarī</s>: "Dear friend! <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, like a moonstone by moonbeams, has been melted by your virtues and cannot bring himself to speak.
The prince indeed wishes to depart; behind him the royal court, not knowing the true situation, waits in distress.
Moreover, even when you two are far apart, this love between you — like that between a lotus-lake and the sun, or between a bed of night-lilies and the lord of night-lilies (the moon) — will endure until the end of the world.
Therefore, may your ladyship grant him leave."
Then <s>Kādambarī</s> said: "Friend <s>Mahāśvetā</s>! This person with all attendants is at the prince's disposal, like his own inner self — what need is there for formal consent here?" And with that, first to <s>Mahāśvetā</s>, then to <s>Kādambarī</s> — being held by her love-tender gaze and heart — he said: "O princess! What can I say? The world does not trust those who speak much. May I be remembered in conversations among your attendants." And saying this, he left the maidens' inner quarters. All the maidens' company, except <s>Kādambarī</s>, drawn by the gravity of his virtues, as if helpless, followed him as he departed, all the way to the outer gate.
When the maidens' company had turned back, mounting a horse brought by <s>Keyūraka</s>, accompanied by those <s>Gandharva</s> princes, he set forth from <s>Hemakūṭa</s> to depart.
And as he went, the daughter of <s>Citraratha</s> was not only inwardly but outwardly too the sole object of all his hopes.
For indeed, he saw that doe-eyed one behind him, as if clinging with the pain of unbearable separation felt in mind; before him, as if blocking his path; in the sky, as if flung upward by the agitation of a heart distressed by parting; and upon his chest, as if stationed there with a mind longing to gaze fully at his face in separation.
And gradually reaching the hermitage of <s>Mahāśvetā</s> on the shore of the clear lake, he saw his own encampment that had arrived following the rainbow tracks of <s>Indrāyudha's</s> (his horse's) hooves.
Having dismissed all the <s>Gandharva</s> princes, saluted by the people of the encampment with joy, curiosity, and wonder, he entered his own quarters.
Having honored all the assembled kings, he spent most of the day with <s>Vaiśampāyana</s> and <s>Patralekhā</s>, conversing with the very same narrative: "<s>Mahāśvetā</s> is thus, <s>Kādambarī</s> is thus, <s>Madalekhā</s> is thus, <s>Tamālikā</s> is thus, <s>Keyūraka</s> is thus."
The royal fortune did not gladden his heart in his capital, as if hostile to the sight of <s>Kādambarī's</s> beauty.
And as he thought of that white-eyed one with a heart restless with longing, that night passed for him while he remained wide awake.
The next day, when the blessed sun had risen, while he was in the audience pavilion, his mind elsewhere, he suddenly saw <s>Keyūraka</s> entering with the doorkeeper.
From a distance, making a prostration with his crown touching the ground, when addressed with "Come, come!" — first seized by his creeping gaze, then by his heart, then by the rising of his body-hair, and finally with his arms — he rushed forward and tightly embraced the approaching <s>Keyūraka</s>.
He seated him near himself and asked, his words seeming to drip with the nectar of joy, their syllables whitened as if by the ambrosia of affection: "<s>Keyūraka</s>! Tell me, is the princess <s>Kādambarī</s> well, with her companions and attendants? And the blessed <s>Mahāśvetā</s> too?" And <s>Keyūraka</s>, as if bathed and anointed by that very smile born of the prince's excess of affection, his travel-fatigue instantly dispelled, bowed reverently and said most respectfully: "She is well today, she whom my lord asks about." And saying this, he uncovered and showed a lotus-leaf cup, its mouth tied with lotus-fiber thread, sealed with a ring-impression of fresh lotus-stalk bracelets set in moist sandalwood paste, wrapped in a moist cloth.
And opening it, he displayed the tokens sent by <s>Kādambarī</s>:
Namely: <s>pūga</s> (areca) nuts — emerald-green, peeled, with lovely clusters — milky; <s>tāmbūla</s> (betel) leaves pale as the cheeks of a female parrot; camphor in thick chunks like pieces of <s>Hara's</s> (Śiva's) crescent moon; and a <s>Malaya</s> (sandalwood) unguent exquisitely fragrant with an abundance of <s>mṛgamada</s> (musk).
And he said: "The princess <s>Kādambarī</s> worships my lord with joined palms through whose delicate finger-gaps stream red rays from the crest-gem she touches; <s>Mahāśvetā</s> with words of well-being accompanied by an embrace of the throat; <s>Madalekhā</s> with a bow whose forehead is bathed in the lustre of the crest-jewels of her nodding peacock-feather tiara; and the entire company of maidens with foreheads whose <s>makarikā</s> (ornamental design) tips touch the ground at the parting of their hair; and <s>Tamālikā</s> with a prostration at your feet, touching the dust of your feet."
"And <s>Mahāśvetā</s> has sent this message for you: 'Blessed are those from whose sight you have not departed, for those moon-cool virtues of yours, which were like moonbeams in your presence, have become like the rays of the blazing sun in your absence. People yearn even for a past day on which arose by fate the nectar of immortality.
Separated from you, the city of the <s>Gandharva</s> king seems as though its great festivals have ceased and it has become listless.
You know that I have renounced everything; yet my heart, even against the will of one who does not wish it, longs to see you who are partial without cause.
Moreover, <s>Kādambarī</s> is severely unwell in body, and she remembers you — smiling-faced, like the love-god himself. Therefore, by the honor of your return, you should make me, who takes pride in virtuous ones, feel honored.
For the regard of noble persons elevates one's self-respect.
Indeed, this affront to people like us must be endured by the prince; it is your very nobility that engenders the boldness of unseemly messages.
Here is the remainder of the necklace, forgotten on my lord's couch, which has been sent.'" And saying this, he unwrapped it from the border of his upper garment — its luster hinted at by the streams of rays escaping through the fine thread-gaps — and placed it in the hand of the <s>cāmara</s>-bearer.
Then <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> said: "This is the fruit of the <s>tapas</s> (ascetic merit) of worshipping the feet of <s>Mahāśvetā</s>, that the princess <s>Kādambarī</s> heaps such an exceedingly great and undeserved grace upon even a servant." And placing all of it upon his head, he himself took it.
And with that unguent — as if the charm of <s>Kādambarī's</s> cheeks had melted, as if her smiling glance had been rendered into liquid, as if her heart had liquefied, as if her host of virtues had oozed forth — soothing to the touch, delightful, and fragrant, he anointed himself and placed that very necklace upon his neck.
And having taken betel, rising after just a moment, resting his left arm on <s>Keyūraka's</s> shoulder, still standing, he dismissed the assembled chief kings with honors duly rendered, and slowly went to see <s>Gandhamādana</s>, the elephant.
There, standing for just a moment, he himself offered the elephant a mouthful of dry grass, tangled with the rays of his own nails, as if a bunch of fresh lotus stalks, and then proceeded towards the stable of his beloved horse. And as he walked, turning his face slightly to either side, he glanced at his attendants.
Then, when the perceptive doorkeepers had restrained the entire retinue from following and cleared them away, he entered the stable with only <s>Keyūraka</s> as companion.
As the stable-keepers bowed with eyes anxious with fear of being dismissed and withdrew, he adjusted the covering cloth on <s>Indrāyudha's</s> (his horse's) back which had slipped slightly to one side, and brushing aside the saffron-tawny mane that obstructed the half-closed eyes, stepping onto the hoof-rest with his foot, leaning his body-weight playfully and slowly against the stable wood, he spoke with curiosity: "<s>Keyūraka</s>! Tell me, from the time of my departure, what has transpired in the household of the <s>Gandharva</s> king? With what occupation has the <s>Gandharva</s> king's daughter passed the time? What did <s>Mahāśvetā</s> do? What did <s>Madalekhā</s> say? What were the conversations of the attendants? What was your occupation? And was there any talk concerning me?" <s>Keyūraka</s> then narrated everything: "My lord! Hear: when you departed, making a sound in the maidens' quarters like the rolling of drums for the march of a thousand hearts with the jingling of her ankle-bells, the princess <s>Kādambarī</s> ascended to the palace pinnacle with her attendants and gazed upon the very path of my lord's departure, grey with the dust of his horses.
And when my lord had vanished from sight, leaning her face on <s>Madalekhā's</s> shoulder, flooding him with gazes white as a canopy of milk-ocean, and with the pretext of a white parasol keeping the sun's rays at bay as if from the moon's jealousy, she remained there for a long time.
From there, descending somehow with sorrow, standing for a moment in the audience hall, then rising — with bees buzzing at the offering-flowers that announced themselves as she faltered in her steps; with her bracelets slipping forward toward her fingertips whitened by the luster of water-stream-bright nails, creating as it were necklaces for the necks of the palace peacocks alarmed by the sound of bangles; and at every step grasping with her hand the white blossom-shoots of the household creepers and with her mind the host of my lord's virtues — she came to that very pleasure-mountain where my lord had stayed.
And approaching it, she spent the day watching the signs of my lord's presence pointed out again and again by the attendants: 'Here my lord sat on this emerald slab-terrace cooled by the spray of the fountain shaped like a <s>makarikā</s> (crocodile) spout watering green creepers; here he bathed at this rocky spot matted with swarms of bees attracted by the fragrance of perfumed water; here on this sandy bank of the mountain stream dusted with flower-pollen, the blessed <s>Śūlapāṇi</s> (Śiva) was worshipped; here on this crystal slab outshining the moon's radiance, he ate; here on this pearl-mountain stone slab stained with transferred sandalwood paste, he slept.'
And at the end of the day, somehow, by <s>Mahāśvetā's</s> efforts, she took food — though unwelcome — in that very crystal-gem stone chamber.
When the blessed sun had set and the moon had risen, remaining there for some time, her body softening as if made of moonstone at moonrise, placing her hands on her cheeks as if from fear of the moon-disk entering her, lost in some thought, she remained with closed eyes for just a moment, then rising — lifting her feet heavy as if laden with the weight of the moon's reflection fallen upon her immaculate nails — with steps graceful in their slow playful gait, she went to the bedchamber.
And having laid her body upon the bed, from that moment, tormented by a severe headache, writhing, overwhelmed by a terrible fever in the form of burning heat, afflicted by some malady, she spent the night in great suffering with eyes unclosed, together with the auspicious lamps, the <s>kumuda</s> (night-lily) beds, and the <s>cakravāka</s> birds.
And at dawn she summoned me and, with reproach, gave orders for investigating news of my lord."
<s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, hearing this, desiring to go, crying "My horse! My horse!" rushed out of the palace.
And mounting <s>Indrāyudha</s>, brought with saddle by the hurrying grooms, placing <s>Patralekhā</s> behind him, stationing <s>Vaiśampāyana</s> to guard the encampment, dismissing all the retinue, accompanied only by <s>Keyūraka</s> on another horse, he rode to <s>Hemakūṭa</s>.
Reaching the door of <s>Kādambarī's</s> palace, he dismounted.
Having dismounted and entrusted the horse to a doorkeeper, accompanied by <s>Patralekhā</s> who was curious to see <s>Kādambarī</s> for the first time, he entered and asked one of the chief guards who came forward: "Where is the princess <s>Kādambarī</s>?"
When the guard, having bowed, reported: "My lord! She is resting in a snow-house built at the lakeside of lotus-ponds beneath the pleasure-mountain of the dancing peacock," he went some distance through the pleasure-garden, guided by <s>Keyūraka</s>, and saw daylight turning green from the radiance of plantain groves, the sun's rays turned into grass.
And in their midst he saw the snow-house, covered all over with lotus leaves.
And emerging from it, he saw <s>Kādambarī's</s> body-attendants — a whole troop — as if water-deities, as if an assembly of <s>Varuṇa's</s> (the water-god's) graces, as if a gathering of autumns, as if a congress of lakes — skilled in cooling ministrations, servants devoted to <s>Kādambarī's</s> body: wrapped as if in water itself under the pretext of moist garments; their limbs whitened by lotus-stalk bracelets held in vine-arms as if by ornaments; wearing <s>ketakī</s> (screw-pine) inner petals as ear-ornaments making their lips pale like parrots, mocking tooth-decorations; their lotus-faces bearing sandalwood <s>tilaka</s> marks as if wearing badges of good fortune; their cheeks bearing dots of sandalwood as if carrying reflections of the moon lingering by day from desire for touch; wearing ear-ornaments of <s>śaibala</s> (moss) clusters that surpassed all the beauty of <s>śirīṣa</s> flowers; with lotus-leaf coverings placed upon breasts garlanded with <s>vakula</s> wreaths moistened by drops of sandalwood juice mixed with camphor dust; with hands pale from constant sandalwood application, holding lotus-stalk wands for fans of lotus-fiber as if grinding <s>candūra</s> cakes in the anger of heat; shielded from the sun by upright-stemmed lotuses, <s>kumuda</s> lilies, <s>kuvalaya</s> blue lotuses, tender shoots, plantain leaves, lotus petals, and <s>kumuda</s> clusters fashioned into parasols.
And saluted by them as they swiftly stepped aside as if in fear of being trodden by his footstep-nails, making way for him, passing beneath plantain arches — whose posts were made of sandalwood paste, whose bells were made of white lotus buds, whose whisks were made of blooming <s>sindhuvāra</s> flower-clusters, whose garlands were thick <s>mallikā</s> (jasmine) buds, whose necklaces were made of clove-shoot and sandalwood wreaths, whose flags were <s>kumuda</s> (night-lily) garlands swaying, whose attendant door-keepers held lotus-fiber staffs and beautiful flower-ornaments, resembling replicas of the goddess of spring — he entered and looked about in all directions with his gaze released.
Somewhere he saw garden-streams running with sandalwood juice, their banks lined with <s>tamāla</s>-leaf hedges, their sandy shores white with <s>kumuda</s> dust; somewhere, on floors of vermilion paste beneath awnings of water-moist canopies decorated with <s>nicula</s> (barberry) cluster fans, beds of red lotuses were being spread; somewhere, crystal chambers with walls whose coolness was perceptible only by touch, being sprinkled with <s>elā</s> (cardamom) juice; somewhere, clusters of mechanical peacocks being hoisted onto the roofs of lotus-stalk spray-houses with <s>śirīṣa</s>-feather-thatched lawns, greyed with the spray-droplets of cascades; somewhere, leaf-huts whose interiors were covered with <s>jambū</s> (rose-apple) sprouts sprinkled with mango juice; somewhere, golden lotus-ponds being churned by herds of playful artificial baby elephants; somewhere, in fragrant-water wells with golden-mortar seats, water-tanks and dripping-vessels fashioned from thick lotus-stalk rods, with bucket-wheel devices strung with chains of <s>kuvalaya</s> (blue lily) garlands; somewhere, illusion-cloud formations being made to move about, their rainbows traced by streams of water poured from rows of crystal herons; somewhere, pearl-necklaces being cooled in pools of liquid sandalwood with pale barley sprouts growing on their edges, dotted with the buds of fresh <s>mālatī</s> jasmine; somewhere, artificial trees emitting large steady drops of water, their boughs made of pearl-dust paste; somewhere, revolving rows of mechanical leaf-birds fluttering their wings and scattering mist-like spray-frost; somewhere, flower-garland swings resounding with the sharper buzzing of bee-bells; somewhere, golden jars being brought in through openings, their mouths covered by overarching tall lotus leaves; somewhere, lovely bamboo-shaped parasols of flower clusters with pillars made of plantain-stalk cores; somewhere, lotus-fiber cloths being perfumed with the juice of camphor leaves crushed by hand; somewhere, <s>lavalī</s>-fruit-juice-moistened ear-ornaments made of <s>tṛṇaśūka</s> (grass-awn) clusters; somewhere, cool medicinal juices in <s>ulapa</s>-grass vessels being fanned by lotus-leaf fans — observing all these and similar contrivances for providing cooling comforts being made by the attendants, he reached the central part of the snow-house — as if the heart of <s>Himavat</s> (the Himalaya), the water-sport chamber of <s>Pracetas</s> (Varuṇa), the birthplace of all moonbeams, the ancestral home of all sandalwood-forest deities, the source of all moonstones, the dwelling of all nights of the month of <s>Māgha</s>, the meeting-house of all rainy seasons, the counter-remedy of all rivers against the heat of summer, the refuge of all oceans from the burning of the submarine fire, the antidote for all clouds against the burn of lightning-fire, the station for water-lilies to endure the unbearable day of separation from the moon — shunned on all sides by fires which, though sun-born, had retreated in fear of its supremely cold touch from the thousands of water-machine streams sent up everywhere; followed as if with bristling hair by plantain groves whose leaves trembled in wind-born shivers of chill; made vocal as if by tooth-<s>vīṇā</s>-playing bees maddened by the fragrance of blossoms; and adorned by creepers dense with unbroken swarms of bees, as if wearing dark cloaks.
And gradually, within and without that place, being rubbed as it were by the exceedingly cool touch applied thickly like unguent, he imagined his mind to be made of moon, his senses of <s>kumuda</s> (night-lilies), his limbs of moonlight, and his intellect of lotus stalks.
He considered the sun's rays to be made of pearl-necklaces, the sunlight of sandalwood, the wind of camphor, time itself of snow, and the three worlds of frost.
And in one part of such a place, surrounded by a retinue of companions — like the blessed <s>Gaṅgā</s> with all her tributary rivers, gone into a cave of <s>Himavat</s> — lying upon a flower-bed beneath a lotus-stalk pavilion encircled by a stream of camphor-juice flowing in a channel-whirl, bound as if with shackles by <s>Manmatha</s> (the love-god) out of jealousy, with fetters of necklaces, armlets, bracelets, girdles, and anklets made of lotus-fiber; as if touched on the forehead by the hare-marked one (the moon) in the form of a sandalwood-white mark; as if kissed on the tear-streaming eyes by <s>Varuṇa</s> (the water-god); as if bitten on the mouth by the wind-god who increased her sighs; as if sat upon on her limbs heated by the burning of passion by the sun; as if seized in the heart by the fire of <s>Kandarpa</s> (the love-god) with outstretched arms; as if embraced on her perspiring body by water itself — her beauty being plundered as if by the gods from every side; weakened in her limbs which, together with her heart, had gone as it were to meet her beloved; bearing what seemed like a heap of pearls, a cluster of pearl strands adhering to the touch of an unceasing necklace, which was actually a mass of goosebumps upon her body pale with dried sandalwood; her cheeks being fanned with compassion as it were by flower-laden bees, droplets of perspiration scattered like a spray by the breeze of their wing-beats; her ear, as if burnt by the buzzing of the bees on her ear-flower, being soothed by a stream of tears flowing from the corner of her eye; wearing in her ear a camphor-and-<s>ketakī</s>-bud as if a drainage channel for the excessive flow of tears; her pitcher-like breasts being exposed by her garment which fluttered and slipped away, as if in fear of her burning heat, set in motion by the shaking of her long sighs, as if her body's radiance fleeing; pressing her pitcher-breasts with her palm as if restraining the wings eager to rush to her beloved, whose reflections appeared in the falling and swaying <s>cāmara</s> fans; repeatedly embracing the frost-stone statue with her vine-arm; repeatedly pressing the camphor figurine with the surface of her cheek; repeatedly touching with her lotus-foot the sandalwood-paste image as a cooling remedy;
being gazed upon as if with curiosity by her own reflection transferred upon her breast, turning around to look; her cheek being kissed as if with longing by the ear-ornament leaf reclining upon its own blossom-reflection; being embraced as if by necklaces whose pearls, their own souls conquered by passion, reached out arms of luster; making a gem-mirror placed upon her breast swear a life-touching oath as if to the moon itself: 'You must not rise today'; like a she-elephant extending her trunk toward a wild garden-elephant approaching head-on; like a doe-eyed woman fleeing from the approach of an inauspicious southerly wind; like the anointing-platform of <s>Madana</s> (the love-god) with lotus-covered sandalwood-white pitcher-breasts supporting her sides; like a celestial lotus-pool with her lotus-tender thigh-roots visible through her translucent garments; like the outline of the flower-bow (of <s>Kāma</s>) with the tip of its bowstring drawn to the utmost by <s>Madana</s>; like the deity of the spring season, destroyer of cold; like a female bee distressed by searching for flower-arrows; anointed with sandalwood yet passionate with <s>Anaṅga</s> (the love-god) — he beheld <s>Kādambarī</s>, a young woman yet mother of <s>Manmatha</s>, a lotus-pool yet longing for the touch of frost.
Then she, seeing attendants who came again and again to announce <s>Candrāpīḍa's</s> arrival, looked at them with the star of her eye darting upward and asked: "Tell me — is it truly so? Have you seen him? How far away is he? Where is he?" — casting his very name-syllables before her as she questioned.
And seeing him approaching from a distance, with eyes whose whiteness spread and grew, that woman of lovely hips — her limbs trembling, supported on the pillar-thighs of new attendants like a newly captured she-elephant, her will overcome; as if being lifted up by the buzzing bee-swarms attracted by the fragrance of her flower-bed who had taken control; her upper garment falling in her flurry, the rays of her necklace upon her breast trying to serve its purpose; placing her left palm on the gem-set floor as if begging her own reflection for a hand to lean on; with her right hand fatigued from restraining her loosened hair, the sweat-moisture dripping as if anointing herself — squeezing as if all essences by <s>Anaṅga</s> (the love-god) through the row of fine body-hairs along the three rippling folds of her waist; her eyes streaming cool water of joyful tears mixed as if with sandalwood juice from the <s>tilaka</s> mark entering her forehead; the surface of her cheek being washed by a stream of joyful water-drops, the dust of her displaced ear-ornament making it grey as if from the reflection of her beloved longing to enter; slightly bowing her head from the weight of the sandalwood <s>tilaka</s> paste on her forehead, with the pupil of her eye gathered at the corner of her long gaze, as if being pulled toward his face, fixed upon it — she rose from the flower-bed.
<s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, approaching, as before, having first bowed to <s>Mahāśvetā</s> and shown his respect, made obeisance to her (<s>Kādambarī</s>).
And when she had returned the bow and seated herself again upon that very flower-couch, he pushed aside with his foot a golden seat with legs inlaid with glittering gems brought by a door-attendant, and sat on the ground itself.
Then <s>Keyūraka</s> said: "O princess! This is <s>Patralekhā</s> by name, the receptacle of my lord <s>Candrāpīḍa's</s> favor, his betel-casket bearer" — and presented <s>Patralekhā</s>.
Then <s>Kādambarī</s>, seeing her, thought: "Ah! What partiality <s>Prajāpati</s> (the Creator) has toward mortal women!"
And welcoming her who had bowed, she said "Come, come!" with affection and seated her near herself, while the curious attendants looked on from behind.
Overwhelmed with extraordinary affection from the very first sight, she repeatedly touched her tenderly with the bud of her hand.
<s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, however, having promptly performed all the courtesies appropriate to arriving, gazed at the daughter of <s>Citraratha</s> in that state and thought: "My heart is indeed most cruelly perverse — even now it does not believe.
Well then, let me probe her with subtle conversation."
And he spoke aloud: "O princess! I know that this illness of intense and unremitting burning has arisen with the love-god's desire (<s>Kāmarati</s>) as its cause.
O delicate one! Truly, this does not torment you as much as it torments us.
I wish to restore your ladyship's health even at the cost of giving up my own body.
Seeing you fallen, trembling, from the affliction of the flower-arrowed one (<s>Kāma</s>), my heart, filled with compassion, seems to fall.
Your vine-arm, bodiless with the torment of <s>Anaṅga</s>, and with a gaze of intense burning, bears a red lotus like a dry-land lotus-vine.
And when you are in distress, even your attendants, by their constant shedding of tear-drops, maintain what resembles the wearing of pearl-ornaments.
Accept these auspicious adornments worthy of a <s>svayaṃvara</s> (self-choice ceremony).
A young creeper adorned with flower-bees is radiant."
Then <s>Kādambarī</s>, though naturally innocent in her youth, grasped in her mind the meaning conveyed entirely through that ambiguous speech — as if instructed by <s>Kandarpa</s> (the love-god) himself with his wisdom — yet not daring to hope that her desires had such scope, holding on to her modesty, she simply remained silent.
She merely produced a smile-glance, without pretext, at that very moment, as if to see his face darkened by the swarms of bees maddened by the fragrance of his breath.
Then <s>Madalekhā</s> replied: "O prince! What shall I say? This cruel burning is unspeakable indeed.
Moreover, what is there that would not cause distress to one possessed of such youthful tenderness?
For to one delicate as a lotus-fiber, even a cool sprout feels like fire, even moonlight feels like sunlight — do you not see the weariness born in her heart from the breezes of shoot-tip and stalk? Fortitude alone is the means of sustaining her life."
But <s>Kādambarī</s> in her heart made <s>Madalekhā's</s> speech itself the reply to him.
<s>Candrāpīḍa</s> too, with his mind swinging on the pendulum of doubt because the meaning worked both ways, stayed a long time with <s>Mahāśvetā</s> in conversations cleverly escalating in affection, and then with great effort extracting himself, left <s>Kādambarī's</s> palace to return to the encampment.
As he was leaving and about to mount his horse, <s>Keyūraka</s> came from behind and said: "My lord! <s>Madalekhā</s> informs you: 'The princess <s>Kādambarī</s>, whose affection for <s>Patralekhā</s> arose from the first sight, wishes her to stay behind when you return; she will come later.' Having heard this, my lord is the authority."
Hearing this, <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> said: "<s>Keyūraka</s>! <s>Patralekhā</s> is blessed and enviable, whom the princess thus binds to herself. Rare is the princess's grace! Let her enter." And saying this, he returned to the encampment.
Even as he entered, he noticed a letter-bearer who had come from his father, whom he recognized.
Holding his horse, with eyes widened in joy, he asked from a distance: "Good sir! Is my father well, along with all his retinue, and my mother with all the inner apartments?"
And he, approaching and bowing, said: "My lord! As you command" — and presented two letters.
The crown prince, placing them on his head, himself unsealing them, read them in order: "Hail! From <s>Ujjayinī</s>, the supreme devotee of <s>Maheśvara</s>, the great king of kings, Lord <s>Tārāpīḍa</s>, whose lotus-feet are made the crest-jewel by all princes, kissing with the circle of rays from the radiant crest-gem of the upturned beautiful head, gladdens <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, the abode of all fortunes.
The people are well, but some considerable time has passed without seeing you; our hearts are violently longing; the queen too, along with the inner apartments, has been brought to despondency. Therefore, let the cessation of reading this letter itself be made the time of departure."
He had the second letter, sent by <s>Śukanāsa</s>, read aloud too, which conveyed the same meaning.
At this very moment, <s>Vaiśampāyana</s> also approached and showed another pair of letters of his own, identical in content.
Then saying "As my father commands," he mounted his horse just as he was and had the march-drum sounded.
And he instructed <s>Meghanāda</s> by name, the son of <s>Balāhaka</s>, a chief commander of great cavalry, who stood nearby, attended by a great cavalry force: "You must go with <s>Patralekhā</s>, and <s>Keyūraka</s> will surely come bringing them this far. Through him, convey to the princess <s>Kādambarī</s> with a bow: 'Indeed this is that nature of mortals which deserves the censure of the three worlds — ungrateful, inconstant, and hard to grasp — whose affections, treacherously false at any moment, disregard causeless kindness.
By departing thus, I have brought my affection to the state of fraud and treachery, my devotion to the skill of false pathos, cast my sweetness of mere courtesy into a pit of deceitful villainy, and revealed that my words and mind are at cross-purposes.
Leaving myself aside, even the princess, upon whom grace was bestowed in an unworthy place, who was worthy of divine honors, has been brought to a state deserving reproach.
For the grace-showers of nectar-glances of great persons, when bestowed in unworthy places, afterwards produce embarrassment.
Surely my heart does not bear the heavy burden of shame towards the princess as intensely as towards <s>Mahāśvetā</s>.
Surely the princess will repeatedly reproach this false one for falsely attributing virtues, for partiality unwarranted by merit.
What can I do? The command of a father is weightier than the power of a mere prince. But my heart, which longs to dwell at <s>Hemakūṭa</s>, has written a deed of servitude for a thousand lifetimes to the princess.
This wild tribesman has not been given leave by the grace of the princess to depart, as a forest-chieftain by a district officer. In every way, I have gone to <s>Ujjayinī</s> by my father's command.
When stories of wicked people are told in passing, may the wretch <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> be remembered.
And do not think thus: that <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> shall live without again experiencing the bliss of bowing at the princess's lotus-feet.
And to <s>Mahāśvetā</s>, her feet should be saluted with my head seven times.
And to <s>Madalekhā</s>, convey a firm embrace preceded by a bow.
And <s>Tamālikā</s> should be tightly embraced.
In my name, the entire retinue of <s>Kādambarī</s> should be asked of their well-being with joined palms, and the blessed <s>Hemakūṭa</s> should be reverently bidden farewell.'"
Having thus instructed him: "Since your friend's resources must not be strained, you should come slowly, gently" — he assigned <s>Vaiśampāyana</s> to the burden of the encampment. And he himself, mounted as before, accompanied by a cavalry force composed chiefly of young horses — <s>Kailāsa</s> trembling with neighs of joy and playful abandon, the earth shattered by the <s>tāṇḍava</s> dance of their hooves, bearing the wind of beautiful spear-creeper groves — questioning that very letter-bearer clinging to his saddle about news of <s>Ujjayinī</s>, though his heart was empty with the fresh separation from <s>Kādambarī</s>, he set forth.
And gradually, through a wilderness where the trees were mostly of immense ancient trunks, where groves were canopied by creeper-arbors of <s>mālinī</s>, where the path was twisted around fallen trees toppled by wild elephants, where thickets of grass, leaves, and wood-splinters revealed the killing-grounds of brave men, where great trees had uprooted creating forest-fortress barriers, where thirsty travelers had broken open <s>āmalakī</s> (gooseberry) fruits and left the split remnants, where the banks were dusted with the pollen of blossoming <s>karañja</s> clusters, where the wayside resting-places of travelers were marked by brick-set dried-leaf seats inferred from tattered cloth-flags tied to bank-side trees and the foot-sore calluses of wandering ascetics cracked open and dusted grey on nearby shoots — with fragrant but tepid, muddy, discolored water in ancient wilderness wells inferred from leaf-bundle knots and grass-strainers of mendicant orders, with scarce water; and with dry mountain streams whose sandy stretches were matted by thickets of creeper-bower tangles and whose banks were greyed with the pollen of <s>sindhuvāra</s> groves dripping honey — through a desolate wilderness whose hidden hamlets among thick bushes could only be guessed from the crowing of roosters and barking of dogs — having traveled all day, as the sun's disk declined, in the twilight's reddish glow, where the trees — stripped of branches, <s>kadamba</s>, <s>śālmalī</s>, and <s>palāśa</s> — with only a tuft of leaves at the crown mimicking a parasol, and where wilderness farm-plots of <s>priyaṅgu</s> mostly, fruiting and pale with ripeness, had thinned the forest — from a distance he saw, bound atop a long-grown red sandalwood tree, a great red banner: festooned with <s>alaktaka</s> (lac) resembling lumps of raw flesh, moist with fresh red sandalwood juice red as fresh blood, with red pennants like tongues dripping blood, and with a black <s>cāmara</s> whisk dark as a mass of hair, decorated on its staff like ornaments made from the limbs of freshly slaughtered creatures; adorned with a half-moon made of bound cowrie shells, its peak adorned as if by the sun and moon descended to protect a beloved buffalo-son; with a fearsome bell clanging on an iron chain dangling from its swaying horn-tip, and with a golden trident bearing a beautiful <s>cāmara</s> whisk of lion's-mane luster, scratching the sky — the banner, looking about here and there as if for an offering of a traveler, he saw from afar.
And heading towards it, going some distance, he saw — enclosed by a fence of wild elephant tusks pale as <s>ketakī</s>-thorn groves, with an iron archway bearing a garland of red <s>cāmara</s> whisks and a chain of black-iron mirrors fearsome as a garland of <s>Śabara</s> heads with tawny hair guarding the entrance; and with a black-stone terrace occupied by an iron buffalo standing with its face downward, its red eyes rolling with greed for drops of blood — here decorated with red lotuses like the eyes of wild buffaloes slain by <s>Śabara</s> hunters, there with <s>agasti</s>-flower buds like the claws of lions, there with <s>kiṃśuka</s>-flower buds like the blood-stained nails of tigers, displaying the violence of offerings which appeared as if sprouting with curves of deer-horn tips, leafing with hundreds of fresh tongue-like sprouts, blossoming with thousands of red eyes, and fruiting with skulls of heads — with red <s>aśoka</s> trees in its courtyard whose flower-clusters seemed plucked out of season by red roosters hiding continuously among the branches out of fear of dogs; with <s>tāla</s> (palm) trees offering skull-fruit-offerings like <s>vetālas</s> (vampires) gathered to drink the sacrificial blood; surrounded on all sides by plantain groves trembling as if with feverish dread, <s>śrīphala</s> (bael) tree-groves anxious with terror, and date-palm forests with hair standing on end from fright — its precincts not deserted, with young lion cubs at play, the pampered pets of <s>Ambikā's</s> (the goddess's) household, scattering pearls reddened with blood from crushed foreheads of wild elephants, pearls seized by bewildered roosters greedy for sacrificial wax — its courtyard made slippery with streams of blood reddened further by the coppery sun, who seemed to have fainted from the excess of what he witnessed — the shrine of a <s>Caṇḍikā</s> (fierce goddess): blazing at the inner sanctum doorway with a pair of door-panels bearing lampblack-flamed red cloth hangings, garlands of peacock-neck feather rings, bell-chains whitened with flour-paste, with a thick iron spike set in the mouth of a tin lion-face giving the door-bolt, and glittering yellow, blue, and red mirror-amulets; its foot not bereft of cloth-offerings of red-paste-dyed rags, as if all animal lives had come for refuge to the threshold-seat of the platform; appearing as if dwelling in the netherworld from the thick darkness formed by the luster of decapitation-weapons — axes, <s>paṭṭiśa</s> (battle-axes) and the like — whose reflections of fallen black <s>cāmara</s> whisks seemed like hair still clinging to severed heads; decorated as if with necklaces of children's skulls by garlands of <s>bilva</s> (wood-apple) leaves interspersed with inlaid red sandalwood gleaming plates and shoots; seeming to exude cruelty through limbs bristling with <s>romāñca</s> (goosebumps) of excitement from the loud and rapid beating of animal-sacrifice drums, with worship performed using blood-copper <s>kadamba</s> flower-clusters — presided over by an aged <s>Drāviḍa</s> priest: his forehead adorned with a beautiful gold plate-covering bearing a <s>sindūra</s> (vermilion) dot applied by <s>Śabara</s> beauties, his cheek-surfaces reddened by the luster of <s>dāḍima</s> (pomegranate) ear-ornaments, his lip-cup reddened by blood-colored betel, his face scowling with crooked tawny eyes — his body seeming to assume the disguise of <s>Mahākāla</s> visiting his beloved <s>Ambikā</s>, wrapped in <s>kusumbha</s>-pinkened silk; the sanctum glowing with the reddish smokiness of dense blue <s>guggulu</s> (bdellium) incense from the moving inner lamp-creepers like fingers of the goddess dripping with the blood of the buffalo-demon <s>Mahiṣāsura</s> — as if threatening, by shaking the trident-staff of the shoulder-throne to scratch an itch, a wild buffalo for its offence; worshipped as if by goats with dangling beards maintaining their vow, as if by mice with quivering lips devoted to <s>japa</s> (prayer), as if by deer wearing black-deerskin robes performing penance, as if by black serpents bearing head-crest gem-lamps with blazing red-crest jewels; praised on all sides as if by a harsh crow-chorus chanting hymns of praise; with its entire body mottled as if by an <s>alakṣmī</s> (anti-fortune) that had dug out the marks of auspiciousness, with pox-blister spots, criss-crossed with networks of thick veins like the web-patterns of lizards and chameleons that had climbed upon it fearing it was a burnt stump — this priest: wearing a rosary like a <s>rudrākṣa</s> rosary placed as a side-tuft on his ear; with a tumor swelling on his forehead blackened by falling at <s>Ambikā's</s> feet; one eye burst open from the application of a quack's <s>siddhāñjana</s> (magical collyrium), making his care in applying common collyrium three times daily to the other eye smooth with the polished wooden applicator redundant; his teeth gradually loosened as treatment for the bitter gourd-sweat of every day; one arm withered and dried from being struck with stones at some wrong place, the passion for massage stilled; his sight in the upper eye dimmed from repeated application of bitter caustic wicks; carrying a boar's tusk as an <s>aśmabheda</s> (stone-breaking) tool; collecting wild castor-oil for medicinal collyrium; his left ring-finger contracted by a needle-sewn vein-operation; his big toe wounded by a silk-cloth cover-chafing sore; afflicted by untimely fevers brought on by poorly prepared <s>rasāyana</s> (elixirs); though aged, tormented by the futile quest for the boon of sovereignty over the southern kingdoms; his fortunes bound by the written-down <s>tilaka</s> (mark) as directed by a poorly-trained mendicant; carrying ink-stained vessels smeared with green leaf-juice and charcoal soot; holding palm-leaf manuscripts of quack-treatises in smoke-reddened lac-ink letters of the <s>Durgā</s> hymns; inscribed in worn-out <s>Pāśupata</s> teachings with the doctrine of <s>Mahākāla</s>; afflicted with the disease of manifest treasure-talk; blown by the wind of newly-arisen talk of alchemical transmutation; possessed by the demon of obsession with entering caves of <s>Asuras</s>; deluded by the desire-fantasy of lusting after <s>Yakṣa</s> maidens; hoarding ever-increasing collection of invisibility-<s>mantra</s> practices; knowing thousands of marvels of <s>Śrīparvata</s>; his ear-cavities slapped open by demon-possessed people chased by repeatedly consecrated mustard-seed blows; with unabandoned pride in his <s>Śaiva</s> identity; avoided by travelers tormented by his clumsy playing of a gourd-<s>vīṇā</s>; singing something during the day alone in a voice imitating the whine of mosquitoes while swaying his limbs; a dancing devotee performing hymns of devotion to <s>Bhāgīrathī</s> (Gaṅgā) composed in his own vernacular tongue; having taken the vow of equine celibacy, repeatedly administering love-charms to aged wandering nuns who had come from other lands; once provoking even <s>Caṇḍikā</s> to loud laughter by his facial contortions in rage from a badly placed flower-offering; once his back broken in a fall during a fight started by a traveler angered when his lodging was denied; once his skull cracked and neck bent from a forward fall when chasing a mischievous boy; once swelling with jealousy and competitive spirit toward newly-arrived rival priests in the countryside; careless from lack of refinement; limping slowly due to lameness; communicating by signs due to deafness; going about only in daytime due to night-blindness; eating abundantly due to his pot-belly; his nose-tip scarred by the nail-scratches of monkeys angered by his fruit-plucking; his body riddled with the stings of thousands of bees disturbed during flower-gathering; bitten by black snakes a thousand times when sleeping in abandoned empty temples; his skull crushed a hundred times by falls from the tops of <s>śrīphala</s> (bael) trees; his cheeks scarred by the claws of bears dwelling in ruined goddess-shrines; always subjected to the mockery of being dressed up as an old maidservant on a broken cot-frame and married off by townsfolk in their spring-festival pranks; rising fruitlessly from sleeping at many a shrine; bearing even his ill-health attended by various diseases as if his own family, displaying even his foolishness attended by many vices as if it had borne many children, exposing even his anger as if it had borne fruit in the many lumps on his body produced by many blows, revealing even his hardship as if many-faced through burn-wounds from lamp-cautery brands on all his limbs, wearing even his humiliation as a stream of hundreds of shoes dragged kicked and pelted by villagers provoked for no reason — this aged <s>Drāviḍa</s> priest: carrying a large flower-basket made of dried forest creepers, a flower-plucking hook made of bamboo strips, never letting go of a piece of black blanket — <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> saw this <s>Caṇḍikā</s> temple presided over by him.
And he decided to halt for the night there.
Then, dismounting from his horse, entering, with a heart inclined to devotion, he bowed to her (the goddess).
And having made the circumambulation, bowing again, wandering about with curiosity to see a peaceful spot, he saw in one part the aged <s>Drāviḍa</s> priest loudly shouting and cursing in anger.
And seeing this, though tormented by the anguish of longing in separation from <s>Kādambarī</s>, he laughed for a long time.
And he restrained his own soldiers who had begun a quarrel with him while mocking him.
And somehow pacifying him with hundreds of soothing and pleasing words, having gradually asked him about his birthplace, his caste, his learning, his wife, his children, his wealth, his age, and the reason for his renunciation.
And when asked, the man described himself. The prince was greatly entertained by him, garrulous as he was in narrating his past exploits of valor, beauty, and wealth.
The tale served as a diversion for a heart aching with separation.
And having become acquainted, he gave him betel.
When the blessed sun had set, and the princes were lodged in whatever quarters were available, and the horses were tethered to posts in front — their spirited enthusiasm inferred from the shaking of their dust-covered manes as they rolled on the ground, having taken a few mouthfuls of grass and drunk water, their weariness gone from the moisture of their bathed backs — and the military men, wearied by the day's march, lay desiring sleep upon leaf-beds prepared near the horses — in the encampment that shone bright as day with the abundant light of many fires that drank up the darkness — <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> went to a bed prepared at one spot before his tethered <s>Indrāyudha</s>, as announced by the doorkeeper.
And the moment he sat down, a sword of sorrow pierced his heart. Seized by restlessness, he began to dismiss the assembled kings. He spoke to none even of his most beloved companions nearby. With closed eyes he went again and again in his mind to the <s>Kimpuruṣa</s> country. With undivided attention he remembered <s>Hemakūṭa</s>. Reflecting on the causeless kinship of <s>Mahāśvetā's</s> favor, he longed again and again for the sight of <s>Kādambarī</s> as the fruit of his life. He intensely yearned for the acquaintance of <s>Madalekhā</s>, who was tender, free of pride. He wished to see <s>Tamālikā</s>. He eagerly awaited the arrival of <s>Keyūraka</s>. He kept seeing the snow-house. He sighed long, hot, repeated sighs. And he developed an even greater love for the remaining necklace. He considered <s>Patralekhā</s>, who stood behind him, a blessed woman. And thus, without sleep arising at all, he passed that night.
At dawn, rising, fulfilling the wishes of that aged <s>Drāviḍa</s> priest with generous gifts of wealth, and halting to rest at pleasing though not particularly beautiful spots, he reached <s>Ujjayinī</s> in just a few days.
Receiving the thousands of saluting joined-palms of the citizens — delighted and flustered by his unexpected arrival — like <s>argha</s>-lotuses (welcoming offerings), he entered the city quite unannounced.
And in the rush of "I first! I first!" — from the retinue that ran forward, overwhelmed by the flood of excessive joy — hearing "My lord! <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> is at the gate!" — his father, his gait slow with overflowing bliss, like <s>Mount Mandara</s> from the milk-ocean, trailing his clean upper garment as it slipped away, showering tear-drops of delight like a wish-fulfilling tree raining pearls — attended by thousands of kings nearby, their grey hair white with age like sandalwood paste unguents, wearing fine silks, adorned with armlets, turbans, crowns, and diadems, making the earth appear as if bearing many <s>Kailāsas</s> or many milk-oceans — bearing swords, cane-staffs, parasols, banners, and <s>cāmara</s> whisks — came forward on foot to meet him.
<s>Candrāpīḍa</s> too, seeing his father from a distance, dismounted his horse and walked toward the earth with his crown wreathed in the garland of crest-gem rays.
Then, with arms extended, called "Come, come!" and tightly embraced by his father, having been held in his arms for a long time, and having bowed to the distinguished ones present, the king took him by the hand and led him to the palace of <s>Vilāsavatī</s>.
Welcomed by her too, surrounded as she was by all the women of the inner apartments, who came forward to greet him and celebrate his arrival with auspicious rites, he stayed for some time engaged in conversations all related to the conquest of the directions, and then went to see <s>Śukanāsa</s>.
There too, having stayed for a long time in the same gradual manner, informing him that <s>Vaiśampāyana</s>, who remained with the encampment, was well, and seeing <s>Manoramā</s>, he returned to the palace of <s>Vilāsavatī</s> itself and performed all the rituals from bathing onward, as if compelled.
In the afternoon he went to his own palace.
There, his mind tormented with restless longing, without <s>Kādambarī</s> he considered not only himself but his own palace, the city of <s>Avantī</s>, and indeed the entire surface of the earth to be empty.
Then, eager to hear news of the <s>Gandharva</s> king's daughter, he waited for the arrival of <s>Patralekhā</s> as if for a great festival, as if for the moment of obtaining a desired boon, as if for the time of the production of <s>amṛta</s> (nectar).
Then, after the passing of a few days, <s>Meghanāda</s> came bringing <s>Patralekhā</s> and presented her.
Having bowed, <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, from a distance displaying his joy with a smile, greeted his naturally beloved <s>Patralekhā</s> — who now seemed to have acquired a new, even greater charm from the grace received from <s>Kādambarī</s> — rising, embracing her with extraordinary respect, and touching the bowed <s>Meghanāda</s> on the back with the bud of his hand.
Seating himself, he asked: "<s>Patralekhā</s>! Tell me, are the venerable <s>Mahāśvetā</s> with <s>Madalekhā</s> and the princess <s>Kādambarī</s> well? And is the entire retinue including <s>Tamālikā</s> and <s>Keyūraka</s> well?"
She said: "My lord! As you command — all is well.
The princess <s>Kādambarī</s>, with her companions and attendants, worships you with her hands joined and raised to her brow."
Taking <s>Patralekhā</s> with him after thus speaking, he dismissed the assembled kings and entered the inner chambers.
There, with a mind barely able to contain his curiosity, with extreme affection, having sent the attendants far away, entering and settling beneath the broad leaves forming a parasol-like canopy of a house-grown lotus-vine, in the middle of one of the leaf-pavilions that appeared like an emerald banner, gently nudging aside with his lotus-foot a pair of <s>haṃsa</s> (swans) sleeping happily, he sat down and asked: "<s>Patralekhā</s>! Tell me, after my arrival, how have you been? How many days were you there? And who remembers us most intensely? And who has the greatest affection for us?"
Thus asked, she informed him: "My lord! Listen attentively — how I stayed, how many days, what the princess's grace was like, what conversations took place, what stories arose, who most intensely remembers you, and who has the greatest affection for you."
"After my lord departed with <s>Keyūraka</s>, I returned in the same manner and sat near the flower-couch. And I remained comfortably, experiencing the princess's graces, ever new and ever fresh.
In short, for nearly the entire day, the princess's gaze was on my eyes, her body upon my body, her hand-bud upon my hand, her voice upon the syllables of my name, and her heart upon my heart.
And in the afternoon, leaning upon me alone, coming out of the snow-house, wandering about, by chance dismissing her attendants, she went to the beloved young garden.
There she ascended the pleasure-garden terrace, white as lime-plaster, as if made of emerald steps like waves of <s>Kālindī</s> (Yamunā) water.
And standing there, supported by a gem-pillar, having deliberated for a long time — though it seemed but a moment — with her heart, wishing to say something, she gazed at my face for a long time with unmoving pupils, with motionless eyelashes.
Even as she gazed, like one resolved to enter the fire of <s>Madana</s> (the love-god), she bathed as it were in the stream of perspiration, became unsteady like one caught in a current, and trembling in her limbs, was seized by despondency as if about to fall.
Then, when I, understanding her intent, my gaze fixed immovably on her face, said 'Command me,' she — as if being restrained even by her own trembling limbs, her ear longing to hear secrets, tracing on the gem-set floor with her big toe as if about to step away, dismissing the household swans with the jingling of her anklets as her lotus-foot moved, driving away even the bees from her ear-lotus with a breeze from her fan quickly waved over her perspiring face, giving a piece of betel to a peacock as if a bribe, looking about again and again suspiciously as if fearing the garden-deities might overhear — though wishing to speak, could not utter even a word, her speech faltering with shame-choked stammering.
And despite her efforts, her voice would not come forth — as if consumed entirely by the blazing fire of <s>Madana</s>, as if carried away by the flowing eye-tears, as if overpowered by entering sorrows, as if shattered by the falling arrows of the flower-bow, as if expelled by escaping sighs, as if restrained by hundreds of anxieties dwelling in her heart, as if drunk up by the bee-swarms that feed on her sighs.
Only, with tear-drops falling unchecked — not touching her cheeks — clear, face downward, she showed an overcast sky as if raining, arranging as it were a rosary for counting thousands of sorrows.
At that time, from her very presence, even Shame learned shame, Grace learned gracefulness, Innocence learned innocence, Wit learned wit, Fear learned timidity, Confusion learned bewilderment, Despair learned desperation, and Charm learned charming ways.
And when, being in that state, I asked 'O princess! What is this?' — wiping her reddened eyes, leaning with her lotus-tender vine-arm on a flower-garland woven on the terrace flower-rail, with one eyebrow arched upward, gazing as if at the path of death, she sighed long and hot.
And when I, imagining the cause of that sorrow, persistently pressed her to speak — rubbing with her nail-tip a <s>ketakī</s> (screw-pine) leaf as if writing a message to be delivered, her lower lip quivering with the desire to speak, as if secretly instructing the bees of her sighs in whispered words, her gaze fixed motionless on the ground — she remained for a long time.
And gradually, again fixing her gaze upon my face, once more washing her speech — smoke-grey from the fire of <s>Madana</s> — with drops of tears falling from her repeatedly brimming eyes, and through those tear-drops, with rays of her teeth flashing in an embarrassed smile of forgetfulness, as if stringing together the original syllables of speech forgotten in fright — she somehow directed herself toward the threshold of utterance.
And she said to me: '<s>Patralekhā</s>! In the place of a beloved — neither father nor mother nor <s>Mahāśvetā</s> nor <s>Madalekhā</s> nor life itself stands where you stand — for you have been dear to me from the moment I first saw you.
I do not know by what reason my heart, having set aside the entire company of friends, trusts in you.
Whom else can I reproach? To whose other story can I relate my humiliation? With whom else can I share my sorrow?
I shall declare to you this unbearable burden of sorrow and then abandon my life.
I swear by my very life — I am ashamed even before my own heart, which knows the truth. How much more before the heart of another?
How will one such as I stain a family bright as moonbeams with the blemish of dishonor? How will I abandon the modesty inherited through the family lineage? How will I direct my heart toward a wantonness unbecoming of a maiden?
I — unsought by my father, ungiven by my mother, unapproved by my elders — I do not send any message, I do not send any gift, I show no sign of favor. Helpless, like a forlorn wretch, like a lowborn woman, I have been brought by that bold and insolent prince <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> to a state deserving the censure of my elders.
Tell me, is this the conduct of great men? Is this the fruit of acquaintance, that my heart, tender as the fiber of a fresh lotus-shoot, should thus be trampled?
The maidens' world is not to be treated with contempt by young men.
Generally, the fire of <s>Madana</s> first burns away shame, then the heart.
First, the arrows of the flower-armed one shatter decorum and such virtues; only afterwards, the vital organs.
So I bid you farewell for our reunion in another birth, for no one is dearer to me than you.
By the <s>prāyaścitta</s> (expiation) of abandoning my life, I shall wash away the stain upon myself.'
Saying this, she fell silent.
But I, truly not knowing the facts, as if deceived, as if frightened, as if bewildered, as if senseless, said with distress: 'O princess! I wish to hear — command me! What has my lord <s>Candrāpīḍa</s> done? What offence has occurred? By what incivility has the princess's heart, soft as a night-lily, been grieved — a heart that should not be grieved?
Having heard, when I who am ready to abandon my life first, then let the princess abandon hers.'
Thus addressed, she spoke again: 'I shall tell you — listen attentively. In my dreams, every day, that supremely cunning one in messages comes again and again and steals my heart; he makes my caged parrot and <s>sārikā</s> (myna) bird his messengers.
While I sleep, he writes assignation-places on the inner surfaces of the leaf-ornaments at my ears — desires of futile longing deluding his mind.
He sends love-letters whose ink is washed away by perspiration yet whose lines of fallen tear-drops stained with collyrium tell of his own condition — enchanting, passion-inducing missives of <s>Madana</s>.
With his own love as if a dye, he forcefully reddens my feet with lac-juice.
Lacking all sense of propriety, seeing his own reflection in my nails, he thinks highly of himself.
When I am alone in the garden, fleeing from fear of being seized, my garment-edge caught on a creeper-shoot halting my flight, I am as if delivered over by my friend the creeper — and that impudent one, toward me who turns away, forces an embrace.
Drawing a leaf-pattern on my breast, he — crooked by nature — teaches my naturally innocent heart crookedness.
With cool breezes from his mouth, like the wind of agitation-waves rising from the heart, he fans my cheeks, which glitter with spray-drops of exertion-dew, flattering my tresses.
Even with a hand empty from the lotus falling, its grip loosened by perspiration — like sprouting barley-shoots — the foolish one makes his nail-rays into my ear-ornaments.
The brazen one repeatedly makes me drink, with a tug at my hair, his own mouth-rinse water used for watering a beloved young <s>bakula</s> tree, fragrant with passion.
The fool, mimicking my style, receives with his head the kicks I raise to strike the palace <s>aśoka</s> tree.
And tell me, <s>Patralekhā</s>, in what way can this one, whose mind is stupefied by <s>Manmatha</s> (the love-god), this senseless one, be restrained?
He takes even rejection as jealousy, even abuse as a joke, even non-speaking as a lover's sulk, even recounting of faults as a stratagem for being remembered, even disdain as unconstrained intimacy, even public scandal as fame.'
Hearing her speak thus, I rejoiced inwardly and thought: 'Ah! <s>Kādambarī</s> has indeed been drawn far by the banner-bearer (the love-god) toward <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>.
If indeed, under the pretext of <s>Kādambarī</s>, the mind's own disposition is truly pleased directly toward my lord <s>Candrāpīḍa</s>, then his innate virtues, tenderly nurtured, have been reciprocated with interest: by his fame the quarters are whitened, by his youth the ocean of love's essence has cast a rain of jewels upon the wave-crests, by his youthful graces his name is inscribed upon the moon, by his beauty his own splendor is revealed, and by his charm nectar has been showered as if by lunar rays.
So indeed, the spring breeze has at last found its occasion; the moonrise has encountered its opportunity; the flower-abundance of the spring season has obtained its fitting fruit; the defect of wine's intoxication has been transformed into a virtue; and the advent of the incarnation of <s>Manmatha</s> (the love-god) has shown its face.'
Then I laughed aloud and said: 'O princess! If it is so, abandon your anger. Be gracious! You should not blame my lord for the offence of <s>Kāma</s> (desire).
These are the wanton deeds of the wicked flower-bowman, not of my lord.'
When I had thus spoken, she, with curiosity, spoke again: 'This one called <s>Kāma</s> or whoever he is — tell me, what are his forms?'
I replied to her: 'O princess! Whence has he a form? He is a bodiless fire.
For: without displaying flames, he produces burning heat; without revealing smoke-clouds, he causes tears to fall; without showing heaps of ash-dust, he manifests paleness.
Nor is there anything in all the three worlds that has not been, is not, or will not become the target of his arrows.
And who does not tremble before him? Grasping his flower-bow, with arrows he pierces even the mighty.
Moreover, for the lovelorn women over whom he presides: as they gaze, the sky becomes crowded with thousands of moons of the beloved's face; as they draw the beloved's form, the earth's surface is not wide enough; as they count the beloved's virtues, the count is too small; as they listen to stories of the beloved, <s>Sarasvatī</s> (the goddess of speech) speaks too little; as they contemplate the bliss of reunion with one equal to their own life, time falls too short upon the heart.'
Hearing this, she reflected for a moment and replied: '<s>Patralekhā</s>! As you describe it, this person has been made by the five-arrowed one (<s>Pañcaśara</s>, the love-god) to be partial toward the prince.
Those forms of his, and more, are present in me.
You are not separate from my heart — I ask you now.
Advise me: what is proper for me now?
I am inexperienced in affairs of this kind.
Moreover, my heart — which has been brought to a state deserving censure from my elders and is utterly ashamed — sees death as better than life.'
When she spoke thus, I said again: 'Enough, enough now, O princess! What is the point of this resolve toward unnecessary death? The blessed <s>Kusumaśara</s> (flower-arrowed one, the love-god), pleased without being worshipped, has given you a boon.
And where is the cause for elder-censure here? For the five-arrowed one, like a parent, chooses a maiden; like a mother, gives consent; like a brother, gives her away; like a friend, creates longing; and like a nurse, teaches the art of love in tender youth.
How many shall I name to you who chose their own husbands?
And if not so, then this <s>svayaṃvara</s> (self-choice) rite prescribed by the <s>dharmaśāstras</s> (law-texts) is purposeless.
So be gracious, O princess! Enough of this obsession with death! I swear to you by the touch of your lotus-feet — command me, send me! I will go, I will bring your heart's beloved for you, O princess!'
When I had thus spoken, she — drinking me in as it were with a gaze moist with the nectar of joy, yet restrained — though the breaches of passion were breaking through despite being held back, a confused flurry of love-manifestations assailing her as if the frost of a hundred winters had cracked and penetrated the armor of her modesty; her sweat-wet garment clinging with joy at hearing the welcome words; lifting as it were her upper garment with the web of goosebumps; her dangling earring-jewel-leaf catching a moonbeam-like ray upon the tip of the <s>makara</s>-ornament as if a noose of death placed on her neck by the love-god — she, removing it, though her inner being was overwhelmed with joy, holding on slowly and gently to the innate modesty of maidenhood as if to a support, said softly: 'I know your great affection. But where can the boldness of a woman's nature come from, being as it is soft as the petal of a <s>śirīṣa</s> flower — especially for those who still have the nature of youth, the maidens' world?
Those women are clever ones who themselves send messages or approach.
I, a young woman, am ashamed to be sending a bold message myself.
And what can I possibly send?
"You are exceedingly dear" — that is redundancy. "Am I dear to you?" — that is a stupid question. "My love for you is great" — that is the talk of a courtesan. "Without you I cannot live" — that contradicts the facts. "<s>Anaṅga</s> (the love-god) torments me" — that blames one's own faults. "<s>Manmatha</s> has given me to you" — that is a stratagem for approaching. "You have been seized by me forcefully" — that is a harlot's brazenness. "You must come" — that is the arrogance of beauty. "I myself will come" — that is feminine fickleness. "This one loves no other" — that reveals one's own devotion and is lightweight.
"I do not send a message for fear of rejection" — that is the instruction of the unawakened. "I would be cruelly indifferent to the suffering of those who depend upon me" — that is excessive familiarity. "You will know my love only upon my death" — that is truly inconceivable."
Thus ends the first part of <s>Kādambarī</s> composed by Śrī <s>Bāṇabhaṭṭa</s>.
